title: Cop31 collapses: why did climate talks fall apart? - The Latest
article_text:
Cop31 collapses: why did climate talks fall apart? - The Latest
Countries at the Cop31 climate summit failed to reach a keystone agreement for the first time in 17 years. The talks, co-chaired by Turkey and Australia, were intended to produce a pact that would have injected urgency into climate action and financing for vulnerable states. Instead, the deal failed after a standoff over fossil fuels and support for countries exposed to the climate crisis. Guardian Australia’s climate and environment reporter Graham Readfearn tells Lucy Hough why there are calls for urgent reform of the Cop process – watch on YouTube

title: Cranberry jam: warming winters and extreme weather threaten a traditional holiday fruit
article_text:
It is harvest time in rural Wisconsin, and the Badger state’s most vibrant crop is painting the rolling countryside a brilliant, unmistakable red.
For nearly three decades, Nicole Hansen has been farming cranberries here. Wisconsin produces more than 60% of the nation’s supply. On a crisp fall morning, we waded into a marsh with her to round up the floating harvest.
“We need to corral all these berries,” she said.
Cranberries are one of the few fruits native to North America. Contrary to popular belief, they do not grow submerged in water; instead, they thrive on low-lying vines in dry soil. But when harvest time arrives, the growing beds are flooded. Specialized machines shake the fruit loose, and the buoyant berries rise to the surface.
Growing and harvesting cranberries relies on a highly choreographed combination of machines and manual labor, but the process is ultimately driven by Mother Nature. “So we are checking the weather, I don’t know, five to 10 times a day because everything we do is controlled by the weather,” Hansen said.
Across the US, that weather is growing increasingly erratic, due in large part to the human-caused climate crisis.
Shifting seasons and unpredictable extremes
In cranberry-producing states such as Massachusetts and New Jersey, record-breaking summer heatwaves frequently trigger fruit scalding, in which berries literally bake on the vine before they can be harvested. At the same time, increasingly humid conditions and heavy rainfall during the growing season create stagnant, moisture-rich environments that invite fungal pathogens, resulting in devastating crop rots.
In Wisconsin, the threats often emerge after the harvest is done. To protect the plants from winter’s bitter cold and damaging winds, growers spray water over the vines, building up several inches of ice that act as a natural thermal blanket.
“So if you don’t protect them, they do get cold damage,” Amaya Atucha, a fruit scientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, explained.
Atucha spends a lot of time thinking about cranberries and the changing climate affecting them. Data from Climate Central shows that winters in the upper midwest are among the fastest-warming in the nation. Cranberry-growing regions now experience an average of 14 more warm winter days than they did in 1970, triggering erratic cycles of thawing and freezing.
“We know for certain the climate is changing,” Atucha said. She pointed to recent years in which unusually warm February temperatures melted protective ice sheets prematurely, leaving vulnerable vines exposed to sudden deep freezes.
Innovation in the bogs
To keep this seasonal favorite on holiday tables, scientists and growers are racing to adapt. Researchers are leveraging artificial intelligence to identify and breed new, resilient crop varieties capable of withstanding extreme weather and disease. Meanwhile, growers are integrating advanced technology into their daily operations, utilizing drones to precisely apply fertilizers and monitor temperatures across their marshes and bogs.
“When you have a system that works and then out of nowhere you change the rules of the game, then you need to adjust,” Atucha said.
Adapting to change is simply part of the job description for modern farmers. And on a perfect autumn morning, surrounded by glassy waters and floating red cranberries, Hansen acknowledged the pull of this crimson tide.
“It’s amazing,” she told us. “It’s a great way to raise a family.”
- Climate Central is an independent group of scientists and communicators that researches and reports the facts about our changing climate and how it affects people’s lives

title: Plant-based lunches could cut Australia’s emissions by 15m tonnes, new research shows
article_text:
Australians could collectively cut climate pollution by more than 15m tonnes – more than grounding every domestic flight – simply by changing what they eat for lunch.
A nationwide shift to plant-based lunches could reduce food-related emissions by 29% – 15.4m tonnes per year – while saving the average household about $611 annually, according to a report by Bryant Research and not-for-profit ProVeg.
Nadia Schilling, the executive director of ProVeg Australia, said the findings highlighted the “huge difference” that relatively modest changes, such as a meat-free Monday or a plant-based lunch, could make.
That might mean opting for a black bean burrito, a poké bowl with tofu, or a lunchbox with hummus and fresh vegetables – instead of a cheese and ham wrap – she said.
“We realise that Australians aren’t going to change their diets overnight,” Schilling said. “This is a really practical change where everyone wins. Lunch is a huge missed opportunity.”
Australia has the highest per capita food-related emissions in the world, the report found. It modelled the environmental, health and economic impacts for a range of Australia-wide dietary changes, finding the shift to 100% plant-based meals would cut dietary emissions by two-thirds, while just switching lunches would cut nearly one-third.
Emissions from domestic aviation are about 10m tonnes a year, according to government data.
The organisations behind the report, which promote moving from meat to plant-rich foods and alternative protein sources, called for a national campaign to increase vegetable consumption along with policy and funding support for plant proteins.
Almost one-third of global greenhouse gas emissions are connected to the global food system through land-clearing, raising animals, growing crops, processing, packaging, transport and waste.
The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) is reviewing the evidence about sustainability and diet as part of the first update of Australian dietary guidelines in more than 13 years. Draft guidelines are expected to be released for public consultation in December 2026.
An NHMRC spokesperson said the expert committee drafting the new guidelines had prioritised information on health impacts but “information about the economic, social, and environmental sustainability of diets was then considered as one of the many factors that influence people’s ability to follow a healthy diet”.
Dr Diana Bogueva, who researches food sustainability at Curtin University, said relatively small changes in everyday eating habits – when adopted by a large number of people – could have a major impact on the environmental footprint of food production.
However, Bogueva, who was not involved with the report, said the environmental, health and affordability benefits of eating less meat depended on what foods replaced it.
Whole foods such as legumes, grains, vegetables, nuts and seeds provided valuable fibre, vitamins, minerals and plant proteins, she said. “But not every plant-based product is automatically healthy,” Bogueva said. “Simply swapping meat for highly processed products does not necessarily improve the nutritional quality of the meal.”
Sustainable eating didn’t have to be expensive, she added, and some of the most nutritious sources of plant protein – such as beans, lentils and chickpeas – were also among the most affordable.
“We do know there are both health and environmental benefits if you reduce red and processed meat in your diet,” said Alexandra Jones, an associate professor at the George Institute for Global Health, who was not involved with the report.
But rather than focusing on swapping out one protein for another, the emphasis should be on “helping people eat more vegetables, legumes and minimally processed plant foods”, she said.
A good lunch could be as simple as an “old-school salad sandwich” on wholegrain bread, with lettuce, tomato, sprouts and beetroot.

title: Failure of Cop31 prompts calls for urgent reform of UN climate summits
article_text:
The failure at Cop31 to reach a keystone agreement has exposed the need to reform how the UN’s climate summits make decisions, say international climate diplomacy experts and scientists.
The talks in Antalya, co-chaired by Turkey and Australia, were supposed to agree a sweeping pact that would have injected urgency into calls for climate action around the world and support for countries exposed to the crisis.
But because decisions at summits can only be made by consensus, the “Antalya pact” was stopped in its tracks at the final plenary meeting, after countries became entrenched. Faced with the final draft of the cover decision, many were angry it did not “meet the moment” of the climate crisis, nor even mention the words “fossil fuels” – an omission seen as a sop to petrostates.
The former US vice-president and climate activist Al Gore said the failure at Cop31 was an outrage and significant reform was needed. “World leaders no longer want to settle for the lowest common denominator. They want real action to implement and finance a just transition away from fossil fuels. It has been clear for years that the Cop process is in need of significant reform,” he said.
He said most countries had come to Antalya to move forward “in good faith” and it was “time that we empower those leaders with a reinvigorated multilateral process that reflects the latest science and represents the will of the majority of the world”.
In the moments after the pact died, the Australian climate minister, Chris Bowen, co-chair of Cop31, said: “The fundamental root problem is that when Cops were created, for reasons I understand, it was made consensus only. That’s a very tough ask when you also need consensus to change consensus, which is a particular challenge.” He said there had been at attempt at Cop31 to introduce efficiency reforms.
The UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, defended the consensus-based approach, saying it had succeeded with the 2015 Paris agreement, helping to lower expected global heating at the end of the century from almost 5C to 2.6C. But as the talks wound up, he conceded the consensus system had fallen short in Antalya.
Stiell said he was championing a review process within the UN climate convention to seek external advice on “areas of potential reform”.
Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said Cops needed to transition from “negotiating promises and commitments that we never deliver on” to a focus on accountability for promises made and their implementation.
Tobias Holle, the co-founder of the NGO group Shifting Advocacy, said Cop31 and previous failures “show that the process is not fit for purpose any more”. He said: “Despite the political will of the many, the few blocking the progress end
 
up winning in a process whose rules and decision-making structures repeatedly allow the lowest common denominator to dictate the level of ambition. We need a structural reform that delivers on climate justice.”
During the talks, Panama released an open letter to the Cop co-chairs on areas on which it would refuse to compromise during negotiations, including that a path be opened up to changing from consensus to simple majority voting.
Matt McDonald, a professor of international relations at the University of Queensland in Australia, who was at the talks, said: “The legacy of Cop31 might be recognition of the limits of this consensus-driven approach to climate negotiations and the development of alternative sites for climate action.”
He said it was “a different world now” than in 2015 when the Paris agreement was forged, “raising questions about the future of this type of consensus-based multilateralism going forward”.
Cop31 overran its official end-time of Friday evening, ending late on Sunday, making it the longest climate summit so far. It was also, according to many estimates, the largest.
The decision by countries including those in the EU bloc, Panama, Belize, Vanuatu, the UK, the Marshall Islands and Norway to formally object to the cover decision meant the pact could not be gavelled through. Some view the outcome as a positive decision to walk away – a “sign of courage”, as the former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has called it.
China, India and a large number of developing countries did not formally object to the text and subsequently expressed their disappointment at the failure of the pact. The Ghana delegation, which accepted the text, told the plenary: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”
Indu K Murthy, principal research scientist at the Centre for Study of Science, Technology and Policy thinktank in India, told the Guardian the Cop process was still vital. “Consensus and multilateralism still matter, perhaps more than ever,” she said. “A majority vote can pass a decision, but it can’t make an unwilling country cut emissions, and countries that keep getting outvoted will simply walk away.
“A rule that protects every nation’s voice protects the most ambitious and the most vulnerable too. What the Cops need is faster delivery and accountability, not a fight over voting rules that would itself need consensus to change.”

title: ‘Difficult geopolitical times’: Albanese defends Bowen after Cop31 deal failure
article_text:
Anthony Albanese has defended Chris Bowen from criticism following the failure of the UN Cop31 climate summit, blaming the result on “difficult geopolitical times” as the Coalition called for the minister to resign.
Bowen served as president of negotiations at the talks in Turkey, helping run the conference with his Turkish counterpart, Murat Kurum.
Speaking to journalists late on Sunday after a list of countries rejected a proposed “cover decision” – an overarching agreement – for the conference, Bowen said “Australia left nothing on the field” but the “red lines” he and his staff tried to negotiate to find consensus between nearly 200 countries were unbridgeable.
The biggest sticking point was whether the agreement would mention the need for the world to transition away from fossil fuels. The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, Norway and Belize told the conference they would not accept a deal without it.
Saudi Arabia and Russia led a group of oil-rich countries that vowed to veto a decision that included mention of fossil fuels.
Bowen told reporters: “I would have been happy with [a] transition away from fossil fuels being in the text, but that was not going to get support.”
He said despite the breakdown, “in the real world” the transition away from fossil fuels was inevitable and happening at speed. He said more than 90 countries had signed a pledge to increase electrification to 35% by 2035 – a step that should help cut fossil fuel use if delivered – but acknowledged the result was “very disappointing”.
Australia was sharply criticised during the conference for its continued support for new coal and gas export developments. Speaking on Monday, Albanese said Australia’s efforts had been critical in building relationships with Pacific neighbours.
“It’s evidence that we’re living in difficult geopolitical times,” he said of the result. “That is the reality. The important work of Cop is the work that we’ve done with the Pacific, where Australia and our Pacific leaders have worked constructively together.
“In order to have credibility [in the Pacific], the entry fee is action on climate change.”
The Coalition’s energy spokesperson, Dan Tehan, said Bowen should “resign immediately”.
“If Chris Bowen does not resign immediately, the prime minister should sack him,” Tehan said. “As the lead negotiator, Chris Bowen is personally responsible for this catastrophic diplomatic disaster.”
The Greens’ deputy leader, Steph Hodgins-May, said it was a “disastrous embarrassment” that Australia had chaired negotiations over the failed deal. In a statement, she said Labor was “not fit to lead – not on the world stage for climate negotiations, and not at home when it comes to protecting Australians from climate destruction”.
The Coalition, and Tehan specifically, have consistently attacked Labor’s bid to host the conference and Bowen’s installation as president of negotiations. Bowen argued for the role – newly created for Cop31 – after Turkey won the hosting rights after a protracted stand0ff.
Tehan did not say what the Coalition would have done differently if he was in Bowen’s shoes, other than saying the opposition would not have pursued hosting Cop or the position of president of negotiations. The Coalition has abandoned its support for Australia reaching net zero emissions by 2050 – a target introduced under former Liberal prime minister Scott Morrison – and promised to abolish Labor’s climate policies if elected.
It has not put forward any policies to reduce emissions.
Tehan said the consensus model of agreement used at the UN summit was “completely and utterly broken”. “Chris Bowen should have known that,” he said.
While the failure to get countries to agree to the “Antalya pact” in Turkey was a significant moment in the history of UN climate summits, the talks did not collapse completely.
The sticking point was the attempt to find language to reflect the “transition away for fossil fuels” that had been agreed to in 2023 in Dubai.
In the final stages of the talks, countries were presented with a text that only referred back to that decision and did not explicitly say “fossil fuels” – infuriating a sweep of countries.
Bill Hare, the Australian chief executive of Climate Analytics and a Cop veteran, said the lack of agreement on the main document at Cop31 – there was consensus on some minor issues – should not be seen as a failure of the entire Cop process but as “a successful defence of the [UN climate convention’s] integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels”.
Amanda Cahill, founder of the Next Economy, was in Antalya to offer advice on elements of the conference dealing with the so-called “just transition” – a wide-reaching set of guidelines meant to protect communities and workers affected by climate change and the shift away from the fossil fuel industry.
“While we didn’t get the outcome we wanted at this Cop, we maintained the global commitment to justice and equity as countries transition their economies to deal with climate change,” she said.
“We’ve got a lot of work ahead of us, but parties have committed to ensuring the Just Transition Mechanism is set up and that countries can get the support they need to implement meaningful and just climate action.”
Adam Bandt, the former Greens leader and chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said countries had “understandably” rejected a pact that he said “failed to even mention the main causes of the climate crisis, let alone address them”.
“The prime minister’s snub of the UN secretary general by failing to mention coal and gas in his speech set the tone early in this summit,” he said.

title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
article_text:
The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.
“The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis, ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they export cheap raw materials, but import expensive food, fuel and manufactured goods, invariably priced in dollars. The charity warned that climate-vulnerable countries are now expected to fund decarbonisation while servicing dollar loans that often pressure them to export fossil fuels rather than invest in green industrialisation.
With US interest rates rising, the cost of borrowing dollars for developing nations is seeing more cash paid to creditors. Between 2021 and 2024, the debt of such countries increased by just 2%, but debt repayments rose by 28%. The UN’s latest figures show that in the global south, excluding China, external interest costs reached $125bn in 2024. The UN’s climate chief, Simon Stiell, was right when he said that developing countries faced a “downward loop”, where climate risks raise borrowing costs, disasters increase debt levels and mounting repayments leave governments with little to invest in resilience. This makes them more vulnerable to future shocks. Climate finance, he argues, “must help countries break free”.
But is the world failing to tackle climate change because governments lack the political will? Or because climate action, among other development objectives, is being pursued within a global economic system whose rules entrench the inequalities inherited from colonialism? That is the question posed by Fadhel Kaboub, an economist at Denison University, Ohio, and adviser to the UN. His answer is that those structures never truly disappeared, but have evolved into today’s rules governing international finance, trade, investment and taxation. The upshot is that the countries least responsible for global warming have the fewest resources to confront its consequences.
At Cop31, Dr Kaboub was among a group of experts arguing for the least developed countries to emulate Mark Carney’s middle-power strategy and employ the same logic of collective bargaining in a world of great-power rivalry. Poorer nations should seek not just strategic autonomy but economic sovereignty. The experts suggested that they pool resources and build regional common markets as well as green industries together. The aim was to negotiate as a bloc with western powers – and China – for technology transfer and investment without racking up further debt. Half a century after developing nations demanded a new international economic order, the climate crisis may be giving that unfinished struggle a new purpose.

title: Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep | Miatta Fahnbulleh
article_text:
In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.
That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. And yet, the Conservatives and Reform UK want to bury their heads in the sand and break the consensus on delivering net zero. But we know sustained climate action can work.
Yes, the world will overshoot 1.5C of global heating in the coming years. But without the Paris agreement, the world would have been on track for a 4C increase. International commitments, finance and adaptation are working, and multilateralism has never been more vital to our future. Every fraction of a degree we prevent means lives protected and communities given a better chance at surviving. Setbacks bring frustration, but resistance is the sign of progress.
Britain has a responsibility to lead, and we are determined to do so. I am proud of the progress we have made to cut emissions by 54% since 1990 and the action we are taking to achieve net zero by 2050. And I am equally proud of our record on climate action abroad. We exceeded our five-year international climate finance commitment, spending £12.8bn between 2021-22 and 2025-26 against a pledge of £11.6bn. Britain exceeded its £3bn nature target and tripled annual adaptation funding from £500m to more than £1.5bn.
And the real measure of that investment is what it has achieved. Since 2011, UK climate finance has helped an estimated 159 million people across the world better adapt to the climate crisis, reduced or avoided 201m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions and mobilised about £26bn in public and private finance.
So, what next? At Cop31, Britain will push for action. And what does that look like? A faster clean-energy transition, cuts to methane, protection for forests and oceans, and better access to finance. The drive for electrification, in particular, is a huge global opportunity. Investing in homegrown clean power is a win-win. It allows us to break our dependence on volatile fossil-fuel markets and protect families from price shocks, while reducing the carbon we use. And through the rollout of solar energy, batteries, clean heat and electric vehicles, communities in Britain will directly benefit from this energy transition through lower bills and a stake in the energy system of the future.
Finally, the Climate Change Committee has warned that Britain must adapt for our changed climate – and we are doing exactly that. We also know that the climate crisis is now a national security issue and we must prepare for future threats. That’s why we are protecting homes from flooding and making them better able to withstand extreme weather. We’re building nine new reservoirs in England to secure our water supplies and restoring the natural systems that help protect communities from floods. I know we have more to do. Here in Britain and around the world, the longer governments wait, the more families will face the upheaval of losing homes to extreme weather and the more it will cost to put it right. The first duty of government is to protect people: cutting emissions and preparing for changes already under way.
I know these commitments feel remote, even when what we agree at Cop31 matters here at home. I understand why people question whether governments will maintain their resolve when politics gets difficult. On the doorstep, people want to see progress, not more promises. So I share here what I say there: I will keep pushing for greater ambition on climate and for results people can see: warmer homes, secure jobs, lower exposure to energy-price volatility and communities better protected from extreme weather.
We have too much to lose by stepping back, and everything to gain from leading. Our security, prosperity and the lives of generations to come depend on what we do now.
- Miatta Fahnbulleh is the UK secretary of state for energy security and net zero

title: How a tiny rare frog became an ecological warning sign for Madagascar
article_text:
As Albert Rakotoarisoa emerges from the forest into a clearing in Mangabe reserve in the east of Madagascar, he sees dozens of holes dug in the marshy ground, a sign that people have been here to search for gold.
“I came a couple of weeks ago, and these weren’t here,” he says as he surveys the damage, counting 40 holes. “I’m really disappointed.”
Rakotoarisoa, 52, patrols the area regularly on behalf of a local group of volunteers and Madagasikara Voakajy, an organisation that protects the island’s endemic species and their habitats. He has noticed an increase in illegal artisanal gold mining over the last year, as the price of the precious metal has hit record highs.
Standing on a felled tree branch amid the holes, most of which have filled with water, he remembers this as a former haven for golden mantella frogs, an endangered species that exists only in two or possibly three sites in a small area of Madagascar.
“I haven’t seen any here since 2024,” says Rakotoarisoa. “The golden mantella is a source of pride for me, because I remember my father telling me as a child that it is only found in these parts.”
The size of a fingernail, and coloured a bright red-orange with black eyes, the frog is classed as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. There is a Malagasy saying: “Rehefa misy sahona menc dia misy volamena”(“Where there is a red frog [the golden mantella], there is gold”).
Its scientific name, Mantella aurantiaca, contains the letters Au, which is also the chemical symbol for gold. Now, the species has become a warning sign of the wider threat that goldmining poses to Madagascar as it destroys the frog’s habitats and populations shrink.
Madagascar, located off the east African coast, is a biodiversity hotspot: approximately 95% of Madagascar’s reptiles, 89% of its plant life and 92% of its mammals exist nowhere else on Earth. The rate of deforestation in the country is alarming. According to Global Nature Watch, from 2001 to 2025, Madagascar lost 5.4m hectares (ha) – 14.5m acres – of tree cover, which is 32% of the tree cover that existed in 2000.
To try to safeguard some of Madagascar’s wildlife and forest cover, the government had created 122 protected areas by 2015. Mangabe, which is also home to 10 species of endangered lemur, stretches over 27,188ha. It is one of five protected areas that have lost half of their forest cover and is classified as critically endangered.
Any goldmining within protected areas is illegal, explains Valéry Ramaherison, extractives project officer at Transparency International Madagascar. Despite this, it is on the rise.
“Madagascar is a poor country and the situation is not improving,” he says. “Local communities, and some authorities, are switching to small-scale mining for quick money.”
About 80% of Madagascar’s population live on less than $2.15 (£1.60) a day. The country is also among the most vulnerable in the world to the climate crisis, with regular droughts, floods and cyclones causing death, displacement, and damage to crops and infrastructure.
Alakambaty, a village within Mangabe, is home to about 600 people, mostly subsistence farmers. It lies two to three hours – by off-road motorbike along a bumpy dirt track – from the nearest town. Hanta Soamalala, the village mayor, sits on a bench outside the primary school, which overlooks houses, rice paddies, forest and surrounding hills.
“The lack of agricultural production is the major challenge here,” she says. “The main reason is the climate. People grow crops but they don’t get the yield they expect. Before, we could predict when the rain would come, we knew when to plant. Since the weather has changed, and we get drought, cyclones and flooding, we are lost.
“We don’t have a solution other than to just accept the situation and wait for the next season to arrive.”
Soamalala, 50, admits this has pushed people to turn to goldmining. “It is both good and bad,” she says. “The mining destroys the habitats of wildlife, but at least it can help people survive.”
Miners told the Guardian that if they found a site where there is gold, it could take a week to gather about a gram of the metal, which is then sold in Moramanga, the nearest town, for up to 480,000 ariary (£83.40).
Most of the gold collected in Madagascar ends up in the United Arab Emirates, says Ramaherison, and there are substantial discrepancies between officially reported gold production and the scale of artisanal mining. In 2023, the UN Comtrade database reported that 1,162kg of gold was exported from the country, while the national gold agency in Madagascar registered nothing.
In January, Carl Andriamparany, Madagascar’s minister of mines, told a press conference that the government had “acknowledged our current inability to effectively regulate the sector and establish a rigorous monitoring system”.
Back in Alakambaty, Soamala heads down to lead a community meeting with villagers and representatives from Madagasikara Voakajy. The rules governing protected areas are read out and people are encouraged to sign up to the local organisation of volunteers who patrol the area for infractions.
Voahirana Randriamamonjy, who oversees the Mangabe protected area for Madagasikara Voakajy, says it is difficult to get people interested in protecting the forest. The work is hard and largely unpaid.
She also thinks there is a lack of education and awareness about environmental issues. “Most people don’t have pride in the biodiversity of Madagascar and this is linked to them not really taking care of the environment,” she says.
“People don’t care; people are poor and goldmining is seen as a way of getting money quickly, while deforestation is to plant rice for subsistence.”
Despite this apathy, the local organisation has 120 volunteers. They are one of a number of groups that work with Madagasikara Voakajy to raise awareness among communities of the forest’s importance. Together, they conduct patrols, create firebreaks, and restore woodland and the marsh ponds where golden mantella frogs live.
Members are also trying to implement sustainable farming techniques and have started making compost and growing plants and trees native to the area in a dedicated nursery.
About six miles (10km) away from Alakambaty, the Guardian spots six golden mantella frogs within a 20-metre copse of trees. A short walk away, just outside the protected area, the landscape is littered with piles of orange earth and tidy, circular holes that descend up to 40 metres into the ground. Each one has steps cut into the side for people to climb down.
As the Guardian approaches, a small group of people run away. A man and a woman in their 20s come back to explain that they do this because their crops fail so often and they need the money. They say they have no hope of finding large nuggets of gold, but perhaps enough specks to supplement their dwindling income from farming.
These scenes are replicated throughout the country. Earlier this month, Transparency International’s Ramaherison was sent drone footage of mining destruction, similar to that in Mangabe, from one of the country’s largest rainforests in the east. The footage was sent by Alliance Voahary Gasy, a coalition of environmental organisations.
“Once someone finds a small amount of gold in a place, the information will spread very quickly and there will be a gold rush,” he says.
“Meanwhile, we have local authorities who don’t have the resources to do surveillance or carry out arrests. In some cases, the local authorities are also part of the illegal activity.”
In Alakambaty, Randriamamonjy accepts there is no simple solution to preventing illegal goldmining and deforestation. She would like to see more stable, long-term funding for conservation organisations, economic opportunities for communities, and action taken against the individuals who finance illegal operations, buy gold and move it through illegal supply chains.
“If communities see tangible and lasting benefits from protecting a forest – income, stronger organisations, secure resource-management rights and a meaningful voice in decisions – while illegal mining becomes harder to finance, sell and operate, then the incentives begin to change,” she says.

title: ‘Legally, they don’t exist’: the hybrid crabs puzzling biologists and fishers
article_text:
Somewhere out on the Bering Sea, hundreds of miles off the coast of Alaska, a group of researchers onboard the trawler Alaska Knight haul up a heap of crabs from the seabed. As they sort and measure their haul, something seems wrong.
The catch, which usually features species such as the snow crab – a species of spider crab growing up to a metre wide with its legs outstretched – or its larger relative, the tanner crab, is instead dominated by an odd-looking hybrid of the two species.
These hybrids carry a strange mix of characteristics: a squashed M-shape in the mouth, a cross between the flat mouth of snow crabs and the distinctive M-shape of tanner crabs, and a mix of red and green eyes, one from each of its parents.
“I was struck by how hybridy they are,” says Erin Fedewa, a biologist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Alaska Fisheries Science Center.
In the region where the ranges of snow crab overlap with tanner crabs, researchers would occasionally find hybrids, though they were a rarity. But in 2025, they recorded more than 13 times more hybrids than the historical average.
After the 2025 anomaly, the scientists waited with interest for this summer’s survey. “A lot of times it takes several years of our survey data to really understand what’s going on,” says Fedewa.
But she adds: “The very first station we sampled, I was seeing all of these large male hybrids. It was sort of like an affirmation for me.”
The 2026 survey showed that the hybrid increase is continuing, and commercially sized hybrid adult males now outnumber snow crabs.
The phenomenon was triggered by an extreme heatwave in 2018 and 2019, when the Bering Sea became nearly ice-free by early spring. The heatwave led to mass starvation and a collapse in the snow crab population, causing the death of about 10 billion crabs.
Early signs of the devastation were apparent in 2019 and became shockingly obvious in 2021 (the 2020 data is missing due to the survey being cancelled during Covid): proof of one of the largest marine mass mortality events ever recorded.
In a study looking at the relationships between the abundance of different crab species and the heatwave, Fedewa and her colleagues found that the absence of snow crabs – which compete for the same resources and might also feed on younger crabs – allowed the hybrids to flourish.
Realising the magnitude of the hybrid surge, Fedewa’s first thought was: “This is going to be such a headache for fisheries management.”
The Alaska Fisheries Science Center has been conducting yearly surveys since the 1980s to assess the populations of commercially important species, such as walleye pollack, Pacific cod, snow and tanner crabs. The survey results are used to build population models that inform fishery managers in setting the quotas. After the snow crab collapse, the fishery was closed between 2022 and 2024, resulting in hundreds of millions of dollars in losses.
In the years after the collapse, snow crabs initially displayed signs of bouncing back. But the most recent survey showed progress had stalled and there was even a decrease in some size categories. Whether this has anything to do with the hybrid boom is not known.
Hybrids now make up more than half of the commercial-sized catch – but they are not officially considered a species and therefore have no set fishing quotas.
“Legally, hybrids do not exist,” says Ben Daly, regional supervisor at the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, who oversees the research and management of Bering Sea crabs, among others. “You’re either a snow crab or you’re a tanner crab. A tanner crab has two red eyes and an M-shaped mouth; everything else is a snow crab.”
So the hybrids can be legally sold as snow crabs, but they also use up the quota, which is still being kept to conservative levels after the collapse. Hoping to capitalise on the plentiful hybrids and make up for the losses of the past years, fisheries are pushing for separate quotas for the hybrids.
“That desire has validity to it,” says Daly. “The problem is twofold. Number one, we don’t know a whole lot about the ecology of hybrid crabs. Number two, snow crabs are still in a very depressed state. And so the risk is, if we set a limit based on snow and hybrids, but the fleet goes out and only targets snow crabs, all of a sudden we’re overharvesting snow crabs.”
The North Pacific Fishery Management Council, which is responsible for setting the quota, is keeping the question open for now, with a meeting in January that will bring together scientists, fishery managers and stakeholders to discuss what it might look like to be able to harvest hybrids.
In the meantime, Fedewa and her colleagues have brought some hybrids back to their lab from their last expedition to try to find out more about their ecology. Nobody is even sure if the hybrids are able to reproduce with each other.
Linking a marine heatwave to such an extreme boom in hybrids appears to be unique in scientific literature, but perhaps that just reflects the difficulty of conducting these studies. Hybrids of closely related species might look very similar and therefore go unnoticed.
“I would be surprised if this isn’t actually a common phenomenon,” says Thomas Wernberg, a marine ecologist at the University of Western Australia and the Institute of Marine Research in Norway, who studies the effects of heatwaves on marine ecosystems.
“The impacts of marine heatwaves and extreme events are pervasive. There’s really no point of the biological hierarchy that is free from these impacts,” he adds.
Amid warnings that the world is on the brink of breaching the 1.5C (2.7F) warming limit, marine heatwaves are expected to become more of a norm than an anomaly, and the effects could be far-reaching, on species and human societies.
“I think this is a perfect example of how inflexible fisheries management is in the US,” says Fedewa. “As these events or these novel outcomes become more frequent in the future, our fishery management system needs to adapt to become more flexible.”

title: What’s left to do as Cop31 enters its frantic final days
article_text:
The end is in sight. If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun).
But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. Deepening the divide are long-running disputes over who should pay what, and emerging fights over the fairness of the transition and assumptions in the underlying science.
I’ve been following the contentious climate talks from afar every day for our liveblog, as my tireless colleagues on the ground have raced from interview to interview. The three big issues frustrating diplomats help the rest of us make sense of how well humanity is doing at keeping the planet habitable.
Here’s what stands out, and what’s at stake in these final days. But first, the headlines.
Essential reads
- ‘Huge experiment in biogeography’: US offshore windfarms are creating artificial reefs
- ‘When it roars, we roar back’: the man who faces Bengal tigers armed only with a stick
- This is climate breakdown: ‘The landslide hit the side of my car. I heard screaming, and realised it was me’
In focus
In just a few years, global heating is set to surpass that dangerous 1.5C (2.7F) threshold world leaders had promised to pursue for the end of the century. Temperatures could still be brought back down a touch after reaching net zero emissions, but the Paris climate target only stays in play if overshoot is limited – and brief.
In what struck me as the most powerful speech of the two-day leaders’ summit last week, Hilda Heine, president of the embattled Marshall Islands, told her counterparts that it was time to “wake up” to what crossing that threshold would really mean. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”
Many countries can reasonably claim to be on the frontlines of the climate crisis but small islands face the darkest future from crossing the 1.5C target, as even a brief period of extra heat pushes sea levels higher for the centuries that follow. A couple of weeks ago, a UN report argued that Earth’s icy regions face such dangerous melting that temperature rise should be brought back below 1C, decrying the “persistent myth” that peak heat of 2C or 3C could be manageable or preferable to rapid emissions cuts.
“Overshoot is not a new target,” said Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, as she called on fellow heads of state and government to cut emissions faster. “It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”
The obvious answer, which scientists (and fossil fuel companies) have known for decades, is to quickly stop burning coal, oil and gas. But while “fossil fuels” made it into the text of the draft deal published on Monday – words that first featured in the final outcome at the 26th iteration of these yearly climate talks – observers fear the Turkish and Australian co-hosts have not done the diplomatic groundwork for such wording to survive.
The world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and seems unable to break free, Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, warned on Wednesday. “We are in love with our kidnappers,” he said. “We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”
The bright spark, if there is one, is that the push to electrify the global economy is gaining momentum. The pledge to source 35% of the world’s final energy consumption from electricity by 2035 is understood to have the backing of scores of countries, though most of them are yet to formally sign on.
Electrification is a threat to the fossil fuel industry – swapping a gas boiler for a heat pump, or a combustion engine car for an electric vehicle, will inevitably mean less oil and gas gets burned. But it is an easier sell than measures that directly punish polluters. Indeed, even many climate-denying governments have built solar panels and batteries with gusto, while deriding “woke” green climate action.
However, how clean that electricity should be is still up for debate. Though the raw efficiency gains from electrification mean that even machines powered by a dirty power grid would be better for the planet than the status quo, campaigners fear not being more specific will leave the door open to new gas-fired power plants.
In just one of many examples of the murky world of climate negotiations, Wopke Hoekstra, the EU’s climate commissioner, expressed solid support for the pledge on Monday – “The more, the better. The quicker, the better. The cleaner, the better.” – but indicated that Europe was open to flexibility on the last point “if, to some degree, a bit of pragmatism is needed to bring others into the tent”.
The climate crisis can often feel hopeless but change – messy, sporadic, insufficient – is happening all around us. Supporting the Guardian’s rigorous journalism that holds polluters to account is one way you can contribute – please consider doing so here.

IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist 
  
Cop31 as it happened: rich world offering ‘crumbs’ to help poor countries adapt to climate breakdown, campaigners say

title: Pacific islanders face a ‘sickening disconnect’ between Cop31 and the climate devastation at their doorstep
article_text:
“I need to go to sleep every night wondering what that means, you know?” says Albon Ishoda, leaning against a wall in a corridor at the UN climate summit in Turkey. “For us, it’s about existence.”
Ishoda is a diplomat who works for the Marshall Islands – a group of low-lying atolls that are specks on a map in the ocean between Hawaii and Australia.
As the Cop31 summit nears its close, with a scheduled finish of Friday but which is likely to push into the weekend, Pacific islanders are becoming increasingly frustrated with the UN’s decades-old system of annual climate summits.
The region has its own cash fund – the Pacific Resilience Facility – to pay for damages from climate-driven extremes and to prepare for the future.
The Australian government pledged US$67m (A$101m) three years ago, but the fund has otherwise struggled for support. It is still about US$300m (A$451m) short of a US$500m (A$751m) goal, and a “showcase” event at the summit with the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, garnered only one new offer – US$5m (A$7.5m) from Andrew Forrest, an Australian miner and philanthropist.
It is a far cry from what has been promised.
“Disappointing is probably not strong enough a word,” Ishoda says. “We have money for wars but not to save communities.”
Ishoda’s sleep has been interrupted by a related issue that is receiving more focus in the fortnight-long talks in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya: “overshoot”. In other words, how far and for how long the planet will experience global heating greater than 1.5C, a goal set in the 2015 Paris agreement.
Scientists confirmed months ago the 1.5C goal would be breached and that a temperature rise of 1.8C is the best the planet can hope for in the near term.
Tackling this overshoot and pushing for countries to transition away from fossil fuels are top priorities for the Pacific. But they fear the process in Turkey might fail them again.
The need to deal with fossil fuels was absent from a draft agreement released on Thursday by the Australian and Turkish ministers leading the negotiations after being included in a first draft on Monday. Critics have noted both countries have substantial fossil fuel interests.
Albanese told the summit’s opening last week that he was “proud to be here fighting for the interests of our Pacific family”.
But Pacific island nations have had an outsized influence on the UN climate process going back to before the first climate deal was agreed in Kyoto in 1997.
The chief executive of Climate Analytics, Bill Hare, a scientist who has been an adviser to island states at UN summits for decades, says “the planet owes them a lot.”
He says he watched Samoa influence talks that led to the Kyoto protocol, saw Pacific nations help rescue the process after talks nearly collapsed in Copenhagen in 2009, and watched the late Tony de Brum, a minister from the Marshall Islands, become a central player in landing the Paris agreement.
“They have pushed the issue with courage, ambition, and integrity, over this whole period,” Hare says. “They’ve done it in the Pacific way, which has not been to yell and scream, but to make the point quietly, consistently, solidly, and with force.”
A key threat to the Pacific is sea-level rise, caused when warming oceans expand and as melting glaciers and ice sheets discharge more water from the land. A 2024 UN report pointed to Nasa research showing that Pacific islands experienced less than five flooding days a year in the 2010s, which is expected to increase five-fold by 2050. The research found that places including Tuvalu, Fiji, the Marshall Islands, Kiribati, Micronesia and the Cook Islands could have more than 50 days of flooding every year.
Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, says the scale of the threat means Cop31 must have “red lines”. If the final deal does not articulate the need to transition away from fossil fuels and agree that the 1.5C target has to be kept alive – even if it is temporarily overshot – then “this Cop will be a failure,” she says.
“If that’s the case we will need to find other ways to achieve this.”
Pacific nations are already looking outside the UN process to save themselves.
Next year Tuvalu will host the second conference of the Santa Marta process, which is trying to get countries to agree to a “just transition” away from fossil fuels.
And an idea that sprung from a Fiji classroom at the University of the South Pacific in 2019 continues to reverberate. Vishal Prasad was one of the students who wondered if, given the slow progress at climate summits, international law might be able to do more to help the Pacific.
“There is immense frustration with the process,” Prasad says.
He says the reason for the slow process is clear: the “interests of the fossil fuel industry”. Its lobbyists attend in large numbers and engage in “corporate capture” of the space, he says.
Prasad is backed by Vanuatu’s climate change minister, Ralph Regenvanu, a champion of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) case who, like other Pacific leaders, has bounced from room to room this week in Antalya. Regenvanu says the region’s nations are engaging in the talks “in good faith” but he finds “great hope” in the potential impact of the ICJ opinion and the dozens of countries who have pledged to work together on getting the world off fossil fuels.
The lead Pacific campaigner at Greenpeace, Shiva Gounden, says there remains a “sickening disconnect” between the negotiating rooms at Cop31 and the devastation facing Pacific communities.
But he says the Pacific will not be “passive victims” of the delays, which he blames on developed countries. “We will secure our survival, our justice, and our financing, whether developed countries find the moral courage to join us at this table, or we have to drag them there through the courts and alternative frameworks.”
As the Antalya talks head into their hectic and likely sleepless final days, there is a push for the ICJ opinion to be referenced in the global agreement at the end of the talks, but its success is far from guaranteed.
Elisa Morgera, a UN special rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights in the context of climate change, says it has been challenged in negotiating rooms. She urges people to listen more to Pacific peoples, describing their leadership as a “gift to humanity”.“All of us will be safer if we learn from what the people who are most impacted by climate change share with us,” she says.

title: Sweden’s datacentre politics are more complicated than they appear | Letter
article_text:
Steve Rose’s account of Sweden’s datacentre sector (‘Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?’, 12 November) is a welcome reminder that digital infrastructure can be developed in more environmentally responsible ways. However, his suggestion that datacentres have become politically contentious elsewhere, “but here in Sweden, not so much”, is a misrepresentation.
 
Consider the proposed Google datacentre development at Torsboda, near Sundsvall, which requires an enormous allocation of electricity and industrial land. The StoppaGoogle campaign, initiated by the regional political party Norrlandspartiet, has been vocal in challenging what this development will mean for electricity prices, employment and regional development.
 
Controversy over datacentres in Sweden’s north reflect wider debate about resource extraction for the green and technological transitions, and the worry that Sweden is becoming an “electricity colony” of big tech, providing cheap, green energy while the economic benefits are realised elsewhere.
 
At the same time, Sweden-based researchers, such as Julia Velkova, and Jutta Haider and Malte Rödl, have argued that the sustainability of digital infrastructure cannot be reduced to carbon emissions and technological efficiency. Datacentres place high demands on electricity grids, necessitating government investment and compromising access for other industries, communities and public services. While these direct impacts of datacentres are important, so too are the downstream consequences that they overshadow, including how digital services promote climate disinformation and unsustainable mass consumption.
 
Sweden’s renewable energy infrastructure does not make datacentre development environmentally or politically unproblematic, but contributes to distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources.
 
Rather than presenting Sweden as an exception to the growing politicisation of datacentres, we should recognise how these conflicts emerge differently in different places, shaped by their histories, infrastructures and political economies.
 
James White and Nora Söderberg
 
Department of Technology and Society, Lund University
