title: Cop31 failed but in ‘the real world’ the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable
article_text:
The failure of Cop31 will be measured not in inches of negotiating text, or bland promises made by ministers and officials, but in lives and livelihoods, in hopes dashed and hardship endured, community leaders from around the world have warned.
“Cop31 failed because it refused to name the issue at the core of climate change: fossil fuels,” said Edson Krenak, an Indigenous leader from Brazil and member of the Cultural Survival network. “This presidency chose to ignore the urgency the world is already living through, turning a blind eye to the people who have died, been displaced and suffered this year alone, because of rising temperatures.”
The Australian president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, did not quite apologise for the failure. “Unfortunately we’re unable to reach agreement on a cover decision,” he told journalists outside the hall. “And that’s disappointing, very disappointing.”
For two weeks, ministers and high-level officials from 190 countries laboured over a few pages of convoluted text, only to produce, at the end, almost nothing. What was proposed as the main outcome, the prematurely named “Antalya pact”, inviting countries to electrify their economies and address the “overshoot” of global temperatures beyond 1.5C above preindustrial levels, was abandoned after a lengthening roll call of countries rejected it, during the final dramatic meeting on Sunday afternoon.
The collapse was almost unprecedented in the long history of Cops, because it was so clearcut. Other conferences have produced mediocre outcomes, but usually tried to salvage some face-saving semblance of unity at the end. But after a marathon final negotiating session that carried on more than 40 hours beyond its scheduled end, a small group of countries led by Saudi Arabia refused to accept an outcome that mentioned the need to “transition away from fossil fuels”.
Normally, as Cops proceed by consensus and even a few holdouts can change the outcome, that refusal would have been enough to force through a weakened final compromise that excised such commitments in favour of the presidencies’ preferred wording, referring only to an “irreversible transition towards lower greenhouse gas emissions”.
Instead, a large group of other countries led by the EU, the UK, small islands and least developed countries, decided they would not accept such a weak deal. When it came their turn to take the microphone, each in turn declared their objections – close to 40 countries registered objections or refusals.
Irene Vélez Torres, a former Colombian environment minister who earlier this year chaired a conference of 57 countries on the phaseout of fossil fuels, said this was the right outcome. “This Cop has failed, not because there are no pathways to advance climate action, but because there has been an attempt to erase from the final decision a reality that science has demonstrated and a growing number of countries already recognise: there is no way to confront the climate crisis without ending our dependence on fossil fuels,” she said.
Yet the developed countries that led the charge are riven with contradictions over the issue, as Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, pointed out. “Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves and blocking the finance poorer countries need to make the transition. Without money and credible action at home, those demands are hollow.”
In place of the cover decision, there was agreement on some side issues, including a “just transition mechanism” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to the low-carbon economy, which was decried as toothless by campaigners. Commitments on finance to help the poor and vulnerable cope with the impacts of the climate crisis were sidelined.
Tasneem Essop, the executive director of Climate Action Network, cried foul. “This was the worst Cop ever,” she said. “We are witnessing human suffering on an unimaginable scale, and we had hoped this Cop would take steps to protect people from the worsening climate crisis. Instead, rich nations gutted the very measures that could have made a difference. Negotiating room after negotiating room, developed countries systematically blocked measures that would require them to provide finance to protect people’s lives and address the climate crisis.”
The result also threatens the “multilateralism” on which Cops depend, which is crucial for many of the smallest nations and disadvantaged groups. For them, Cops are the only forum in which they can confront the authors of the fossil fuel crisis – the rich nations and petro states which have benefited from coal, oil and gas up to now.
“Despite the discouragement we feel today, we will keep betting on multilateralism,” said Juan Carlos Jintiach Arcos, the executive secretary of the Global Alliance of Territorial Communities. “We start from a clear premise: multilateralism is not built by political leaders alone. We remain hopeful that the world’s governments will find the courage to join us in this fight.”
The question now is how the world can put this right. For that, what is happening outside the windowless air-conditioned conference halls of Cop may be far more important than any Cop decision, or lack of one.
Renewable power has overtaken coal in China, reaching 60% of generation capacity, investment in clean energy around the world is twice that into fossil fuels, and electric vehicles have taken off, making up a third of new car sales in Europe and a majority in many other countries around the world, from China to Vietnam, Singapore and Iceland.
As Bowen said, in his final address: “The transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is inevitable. It’s happening, it’s happening at speed, and it’s irreversible.”

title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
article_text:
China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.
Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”
China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.
At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.
But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.
In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”
Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.
While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.
But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.
Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.
Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.
China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.
One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.
Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”
China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.
Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.
Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”
Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”
Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a new draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
article_text:
The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.
The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.
Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.
“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.
Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.
Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.
By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.
In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.
As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.
The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.
This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.
The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.
Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.
The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

title: Passing bill to speed up gas projects and datacenters would be ‘serious mistake’, Al Gore says
article_text:
It would be a “serious mistake” to pass a contentious bipartisan bill to speed up energy projects and datacenters that has divided Democrats and environmentalists, Al Gore said.
The legislation, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (Baaja), will make it easier to build large infrastructure projects in the US, from oil and gas pipelines and datacenters to crucial clean energy components such as solar and wind power and transmission lines, scaling back environmental protections and legal challenges in order to do so.
The permitting bill, devised by a group of Republicans and Democrats, passed a procedural vote in the US Senate last week, but has split Democrats and green groups over whether its trade-offs are worth supporting. Gore, the former US vice-president, said he is opposed to the bill and urged a rethink.
“I think it would be a serious mistake, particularly in the wake of the astonishing election results last week,” Gore, referencing Democrats’ sweeping midterm wins, said at the Cop31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.
“The fact that President Trump endorsed it enthusiastically is a clue, the fact that the American Petroleum Institute is giving out free tacos in Washington to support it is also a clue. I hope they reconsider because I think it would be a very, very serious mistake.”
Trump, who has repeatedly attempted to halt clean energy projects in the US, said last week wind turbines are a “major loser” and that he will prevent any more being built, even as the bill to sweep away blockages to clean energy is being considered.
“Trump will implement any legislation given to him in a way that continues to redeem his unethical pledge to the fossil fuel industry during his campaign,” Gore said, referencing Trump’s promise to provide help to oil and gas executives in return for donations prior to the 2024 election.
“The president of the United States is in charge of implementing whatever legislation is passed and he doesn’t play by the rules, he doesn’t respect the law and it’s not a mystery how he would try to implement this legislation,” Gore said. “It would lock in a lot of new pipelines and fossil fuel facilities. And we will have a chance with the new Congress and the new balance of power in the US government to do a much better job.”
But while Democrats will be able to craft a far more renewables-friendly permitting bill when they gain control of Congress in January, proponents of Baaja point out that support from Trump and Republicans will likely wither, meaning there will be no legislation at all to help stop wind and solar projects being bogged down in lengthy reviews, with new generation struggling to bring clean electricity to Americans due to a lack of transmission lines across the country.
A final Senate vote is expected this week and if that passes it would move to the House.
Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic senator and longtime climate advocate who helped craft the bill, said he was working to improve the legislation but rejected Gore’s criticism.
“Mr Gore neither spoke to Senator [Martin] Heinrich or me or our teams before he reached that conclusion,” Whitehouse, who is also at Cop31, said. Whitehouse said he was working on “a variety of amendments to see what can be done to shore up potential holes in the bill” including provisions that would prevent Trump from arbitrarily blocking clean energy developments.
“There was a huge surge of misinformation that came kind of immediately after the text was released … we have had lots of exaggerated fears,” Whitehouse added about the criticism of the bill from some Democrats and green groups that environmental protections were being gutted for a modest reduction in greenhouse gas pollution.
The bill could result in as much as 1.5bn tons of emissions reductions by 2040, according to one analysis, and Whitehouse said he hoped amendments would increase this total.
Whether or not this is enough pollution reduction to justify environmental rollbacks has cut to the heart of tension in the broader green movement over whether to prioritize the climate crisis even if this means all sorts of new infrastructure that may impact ecosystems and communities.
“The prospect of losing tools to slow down and stop the cruelest projects should be haunting everyone,” said Abigail Dillen, president of Earthjustice, which opposes Baaja.
For Whitehouse, though, tackling the climate crisis is paramount. “Nothing is going to be more devastating to the environment than continuing on our pace of climate change, by like a factor of 100,” he said.
“Clean energy development is wildly outpacing fossil fuel development now. In the old days the developers were almost always the bad guys and a mindset developed around that pattern,” the senator added.
“But that has now shifted and developers are 90%-plus likely to be the good guys in the energy space,” Whitehouse said. “I think if you have a gigaton scale decrease of emissions available, it’s important to grab it while you can.”
When Democrats take control of Congress there will be “far bigger environmental and climate fish to fry than just this bill”, Whitehouse added. “I think this is step one. We have to keep going because we are failing right now. We are failing to meet the obligations we have.”

title: Great Britain’s oldest renewables projects could rake in nearly £9bn next year
article_text:
Great Britain’s oldest renewable energy projects are likely to rake in a near £9bn windfall next year because of soaring market prices, according to independent analysis.
The research has revealed that almost a third of the UK’s wind and solar farms that rely on the government’s legacy renewables subsidy scheme are in line for soaring subsidy payments as officials grapple with plans to lower the country’s energy costs.
Renewable energy projects built between 2003 and 2014 are expected to claim £4.5bn in subsidies over the next financial year, on top of £4.2bn in wholesale market revenue. The analysis showed developers will receive almost 50% more than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent gas prices soaring in 2022.
The analysis by the Energy Competitiveness Unit (ECU), a non-partisan research and policy project, said the legacy support scheme – which is paid via taxes and energy bills – must be reformed “if we are serious about getting costs of the electricity system down in the short and medium term”.
Unlike newer renewable energy projects that earn fixed-price subsidies for their generation, older projects access support via the renewables obligation (RO) scheme, which provides payments on top of what developers earn via the wholesale market, meaning that higher gas market prices lead to higher subsidy costs for renewables.
The scheme was credited with kickstarting the UK’s renewable energy industry when it was put in place almost 25 years ago, but the ECU said it “has been allowed to persist unsustainably”.
Andrew O’Brien, the ECU director, told the Guardian that the rise in wholesale prices over recent years has meant that many renewable energy developers are earning “well above what they could reasonably have expected” when first taking the decision to invest in the projects.
The government announced last year that it would remove three-quarters of the RO scheme’s costs from home energy bills, and move these levies into general taxation from April 2026 to help temper the steep rise in energy bills.
The government later warned that legacy generators could face higher windfall taxes unless they give up the existing RO scheme in favour of a new partially fixed subsidy contract as part of its plans to protect bill payers.
The ECU believes that the government’s consultation on plans to fix the generators’ wholesale revenues to help to weaken the link between volatile global gas markets and the UK’s electricity costs “falls short”. It argues ministers should go further to fix their subsidy payments and create a new scheme.
Since 2013, renewable energy developers have been required to compete in an auction to secure a contract for a fixed price for each megawatt-hour of electricity generated, known as a contract for difference (CfD), which means costs remain fixed regardless of global markets.
Under an alternative proposal set out in the ECU’s research, the government could cut electricity costs by £3.8bn next year, and £9.2bn over 10 years, if all generators moved on to an entirely fixed-price contract, which it calls a fair value CfD.
The new private law contracts could also offer a degree of legal protection against the political risk that any potential future net zero sceptic government could dismantle renewable energy support through the government’s RO scheme, a threat signalled by the rightwing populist Reform UK party.
“It is in the interests of everyone – investors, generators, businesses, households and government – to get a credible long-term plan in place that can withstand shocks in this increasingly uncertain world,” the ECU said.
In his budget speech last month, the chancellor, John Healey, said: “We will further break the grip of international gas prices on our bills by moving more of our old renewables on to fixed-price contracts.”
Tara Singh, the chief executive of RenewableUK, said the renewable energy projects were still helping to keep a lid on bills by “pushing expensive gas off the system”.
Singh said: “UCL found wind has saved consumers £100bn since 2010 even allowing for support schemes like the RO by reducing the need for expensive imports.”
She added that the government’s windfall tax, which took effect from July, has meant that renewable energy projects using the RO scheme pay the Treasury up to 80p of every additional pound it earns from market prices above £82.61 per megawatt hour.
“To put this into context, the average wholesale price of electricity over the last 12 months is over £100 per megawatt hour, and frequently higher than that,” she said.
“The fastest way to protect consumers from future price shocks is to build more cheap, homegrown renewable power.”

title: California governor Gavin Newsom endorses global fossil fuel phaseout
article_text:
The leader of the world’s fourth-biggest economy, California governor Gavin Newsom, has explicitly endorsed a global phaseout of the fossil fuels that drive climate breakdown.
Newsom said that California is “100%” behind the efforts of the so-called Santa Marta coalition, a group of more than 50 countries that includes many of the world’s largest economies, to transition away from oil, gas and coal toward solar, wind, batteries and other non-carbon energy sources.
Speaking at the Cop31 UN climate summit on Thursday, Newsom said: “When you have a product that is obviously superior, which clean energy is for the climate and the economy, why wouldn’t you make that shift as quickly as possible?”
As the head of America’s most populous and economically powerful state, Newsom is the most prominent US politician at Cop31, a process the Trump administration continues to boycott.
Newsom, a Democrat, is widely expected to run for president in 2028. His statement raises the possibility that the US, the world’s biggest economy and largest historical emitter of planet-warming gases, could join the Santa Marta coalition if he wins the presidency two years from now.
More than 80 countries wanted last year’s COP30 to begin to develop a global “roadmap” to phase out fossil fuels. A handful of petrostates led by Saudi Arabia blocked that effort, relying on the disputed notion that decisions at UN climate summits can only be made by consensus. Undaunted, countries favoring a roadmap met in April in Santa Marta, Colombia, to begin designing a phaseout on their own.
“Love it”, Newsom said of the challenge that this Santa Marta “coalition of the willing” is posing to the US and other states intent on keeping the world burning fossil fuels.
The coalition is in effect no longer allowing petrostates to employ procedural tricks and endless talk to prevent what scientists say is imperative: rapidly phasing out fossil fuels. Instead, this critical mass of countries, which includes Germany, France, Brazil and the Netherlands – with additional countries, perhaps including the UK, expected to join later in Cop31 – is proceeding on its own with plans to transition away from fossil fuels, hoping that its example and economic power will lead others to follow suit.
“You don’t ask drug dealers to vote for Prohibition, and you won’t get petrostates to agree to phase out fossil fuels,” said Mohamed Nasheed, the former president of the Maldives, who once convened a cabinet meeting underwater to dramatize the plight of low-lying island nations like his. “Countries wishing to phase out fossil fuels should just go ahead and do it,” Nasheed said.
Newsom’s statement could add momentum to a CopP31 summit that has been widely expected to yield modest progress at best. The governor’s comments follow two political earthquakes that also raised hopes of a new era in global climate politics. First came the surprising re-election of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil in October, then the crushing rebuke of Trump and his Republican Congress in the US midterm elections in early November.
What makes the Santa Marta coalition’s vision more than a pipe dream is the coalition’s economic might. Collectively, the 80-plus countries that wanted a phaseout framework at Cop30 amount to the biggest economic superpower on Earth.
If the coalition can begin implementing a credible transition away from fossil fuels, it “would send an unmistakable message that the age of oil, gas and coal is ending, and the smart money is shifting,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the non-profit Power Shift Africa. Governments and financial markets around the world would be put on notice that staying invested in fossil fuels will be an increasingly risky proposition that could leave them holding trillions of dollars of stranded assets.
Thus far, Germany, the world’s third-biggest economy, has committed to phasing out fossil fuels by 2045. France, the world’s sixth-biggest economy, and the Netherlands, the 18th-biggest, have released phaseout plans as well.
California’s clean energy record aligns with the one policy goal that, analysts say, Cop31’s final agreement might endorse: a commitment to obtain 35% of the world’s energy from electricity by 2035. California’s economy has run on 100% clean electricity nine out of every 10 days during much of 2026, with batteries emerging as “a gamechanger”, as Newsom described it. As the costs of clean energy continue to fall, Newsom expects more counties to follow California’s example because “the markets are moving in our direction”.
The midterms also brought to power scores of climate champions at the state and local level. In Texas, the US’s second-largest state economy after California, the new governor is Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who shunned contributions from the fossil fuel industry that has long dominated her state. In all, 29 states will have Democratic governors who, among other things, could block datacenters.
Humanity is in “a final battle against the evil forces” trying to keep the world burning fossil fuels, said Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. As the Nepal glacier disaster and 50,000 extreme heat deaths in Europe this summer illustrate, climate breakdown is already wreaking terrible damage. Nevertheless, Rockstrom added, “89% of citizens across the world trust science [and] want action. We are a majority power that can have confidence we have a collective global community that really wants this to succeed – and that it isn’t too late.”
- Mark Hertsgaard is the executive director of Covering Climate Now and the environment correspondent for the Nation. He has covered UN climate summits since the 1992 Earth summit

title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
article_text:
‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms.
One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. The wood is not EcoDataCenter’s only claim to sustainability; it is more than just cosmetic, says Wernvik, the company’s chief external relations and sustainability officer. “Compared with a traditional datacentre built with steel and concrete, we lower the embodied carbon of the full structure by three times.” With a complex the size of a football pitch, that is a lot of wood, but, says Wernvik, “the amount of timber one of our datacentres uses takes the Swedish forest about 10 to 15 minutes to grow back”.
Datacentres have become a dirty word and a political issue in much of the world – especially the US, where opposition to them was said to be a factor in the recent midterm elections – but here in Sweden, not so much.
There is a familiar litany of reasons why datacentres are bad: they are being built without the consent or knowledge of local people; they consume vast amounts of land, electricity and water, with knock-on effects for communities and the environment; they provide no jobs and enrich rapacious tech companies.
What’s remarkable is how little any of those arguments apply in Sweden, especially here in Falun, a former copper-mining town a few hours north of Stockholm. If your abiding image of a datacentre is something like xAI’s Colossus facility in Tennessee, built at lightning speed with little public notice, partly powered by banks of unpermitted, methane gas-burning temporary generators, releasing huge amounts of CO2 and harmful pollutants into the atmosphere and the community, then EcoDataCenter is practically the polar opposite. “I’m biased, but we believe that we build datacentres in a somewhat different way,” says Wernvik.
For starters, the company’s electricity supply is 100% renewable: 75% from hydroelectric power and 25% from wind. Sweden’s power mix as a whole is virtually carbon-free – just 1% of it comes from fossil fuels (in the EU as a whole, the figure is 29%, in the US it is 55%). In rural areas like Falun, there is sometimes too much electricity being generated by nearby hydroelectric, solar and wind, so power-hungry datacentres are actually helpful in balancing the grid.
Conditions for datacentres are pretty good in Sweden as a whole. The cold northern climate means less cooling is required; the energy is not only green, it is cheap and reliable; there is plenty of water and space; and the country is relatively politically stable and well-regulated – as Wernvik puts it, “it’s very hard to develop something in Sweden where there’s not a consensus”.
Energy is still a concern at EcoDataCenter, considering this place has a capacity of 80MW (the equivalent of about 60,000 homes). There are two key measures of datacentre performance. One is carbon usage effectiveness (CUE): the carbon emissions for each kWh of energy consumed. The average for US datacentres is 414gCO2/kWh, the European Union’s is 263gCO2/kWh, EcoDataCenter’s is 1.17gCO2/kWh. Another key measure is power usage effectiveness (PUE); how efficiently the datacentre uses the power going into it. The EU average is 1.36 (where a score of 1 would be 100% efficiency), EcoDataCenter’s is 1.15. The company is bringing down both its CUE and PUE year by year, according to EcoDataCenter’s sustainability report.
The primary use for energy is powering the graphics processing units – the expensive chips that do the computing, mostly made by the US company Nvidia. (Wernvik reminds me that although 70% of their computing power goes towards AI, almost everything online is run through datacentres somewhere, from banking transactions to streaming TV.) The supply must be constant – even a small drop in current for a few milliseconds could be consequential – so there are numerous backup generators on site, but even these are fuelled by hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), a biofuel made from waste vegetable oil and animal fat, so also fossil fuel-free.
The other main energy use is cooling; removing the vast amounts of heat the chips generate. This is where controversies have arisen in the US over extracting from the local water supply, but it is less of an issue here, says Wernvik. The Swedish climate means less cooling is required, and there is plenty of water around (they get most of theirs from a nearby lake that was once used for drinking water). On a dreary, rainy day, no water is needed: the air is cold enough already (15C – anything below 20C will do). They simply have to pipe it around the building. On days when it is hot, or there is surplus electricity to use, there are electrically powered chillers on the roofs that cool air using a mist of water before it is circulated around the buildings.
The future, however, lies in liquid cooling – where the heat from the chips is transferred directly to liquid, rather than through the air. The latest generation of chips require this, Wernvik explains, as we walk through a spotlessly clean room containing several fridge-sized racks of chips, arranged in two parallel rows. They take up about the same amount of space as a bus. The noise is deafening (but inaudible outside), the chips themselves are barely visible behind a spaghetti of cables and cooling tubes connected to the backs of the server racks. It is a closed-loop system, so it does not use any external water, he says. “Each rack here is basically 25 saunas that we need to cool away and keep at about 27 degrees for it to not burn up inside,” says Wernvik. “That’s the whole engineering challenge we’re trying to solve.”
These particular Blackwell chips are powering DeepL, the German-based AI translation platform. Some of EcoDataCenter’s clients are confidential; declared ones include US cloud computing company CoreWeave, French AI firm Mistral, and research institutes including the universities of Hull and York. Supporting sovereign European tech is one of their key aims, Wernvik says.
The final part of the energy equation is excess heat, which EcoDataCenter reuses as much as possible. Much of it is used to dry wood pellets – a byproduct of the timber industry. The pellets go into incinerators in populated areas to provide heating. There is one right next door, which is no coincidence. (Admittedly, burning them emits CO2, but given the circular nature of the timber industry, they are arguably carbon-neutral.)
The rest of the heat (such as from the liquid cooling) goes directly into the local district heating system in Falun. Since the 1950s, Sweden has been building district heating networks across the country, where water is heated at large, centralised boilers, rather than in individual homes, then piped around towns and cities in underground pipes, typically at 60C to 80C. Homes and businesses extract the heat via a heat exchanger on their property. Already, district heating systems make use of excess heat from wastewater, sewage and supermarket refrigerators; datacentres are now another source to add to the mix.
There’s another aspect of EcoDataCenter’s operation that stands out. While datacentres are being imposed on many communities from the outside, in Falun it was practically the opposite. The project was initiated by local government, says Wernvik, “so the idea from the beginning was very much based on, how do we integrate a datacentre in the local community in order for it to fit the municipality?” This was in 2010, long before the AI revolution. The municipality (like a local council) decided the project would be better handled by a private company, which led to the formation of EcoDataCenter in 2014. The first part of the Falun site was up and running in 2019. The final phases are still under construction.
Local benefits were built in from the outset: 90% of its suppliers are sourced locally and 60% of its capital expenditure is spent locally, Wernvik says. It invests in local education and training, including sponsoring local sports teams and youth activities.
Local integration is even more evident at EcoDataCenter’s second site, in the industrial city of Borlänge, about a 20-minute drive away. This facility, the first phase of which will open in 2027, has a capacity of 240MW – three times larger than Falun. And the site is enormous: 200,000 sq m. In Borlänge, by contrast, they are building on a brownfield site. Poetically, perhaps, it used to be a paper mill, which closed in 2021. A datacentre is a good replacement: it can plug into the existing industrial infrastructure in much the same way – the power grid, the nearby water supply, the district heating. It will also employ 200 to 300 people, roughly the same number that worked at the paper mill before it closed, says Wernvik. “The discussion that datacentres don’t generate that amount of jobs, that needs to be put in context. There are a lot of different datacentres.”
In Stockholm, the datacentre strategy is different, but no less joined up. Sweden’s capital has become something of a European tech centre in its own right, and demand for datacentres is high. Stockholm Data Parks – a joint initiative by the city council and the city’s energy, power grid and fibre optic companies – was founded in 2014 as “a one-stop shop in order to make it easier to attract datacentre operators,” explains Michael Gullberg, product manager at energy company Stockholm Exergi. They free up suitable land, and again, the emphasis is on sustainability, including clean power (the city hopes to be net zero by 2035) and recycling waste heat. Stockholm claims to have the world’s largest district heating system, with more than 3,000 km of pipes, serving close to 90% of the capital. There are about 50 small-scale datacentres in the region (typically less than 20MW), and about 20 are connected to the district heating. They contribute about 1.5% of the city’s annual heat demand, which might not sound much, “but 110 gigawatt-hours of recovered heat is still a decent amount, because the system is so vast,” says Gullberg.
I visit one such facility in Kista, a suburb north of the city centre that has become Stockholm’s tech hub. It is an unobtrusive shed on an industrial estate, with a capacity of 12MW. Crucially, it is right next door to a district heating plant, so the datacentre basically pipes its heated water over the fence. It’s a win-win, says Sandra Karlsson, senior public affairs manager: “When they need to do district heating, they don’t need to boil the water from six degrees, they get it at 30 degrees from us, so they save a lot of energy.” In return, it takes in cold water from the district heating plant, which it uses for cooling.
This datacentre is run by atNorth, a company that began in Iceland, and now has 13 datacentres running or under construction across Sweden, Iceland, Norway, Denmark and Finland. Conditions are similar to Sweden in all these countries, says atNorth’s CEO, Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson: renewable power, reliable grids, district heating, “as well as the crappy weather that we have. We barely can live there as human beings, but datacentres love it.” As with EcoDataCenter, it claims to put sustainability and community engagement to the fore, investing and employing locally, using resources efficiently.
In terms of heat recovery, it’s a bit of a catch-22, Kristinsson points out: larger datacentres must be built in more remote areas, where there is less need for district heating, and vice versa. So they have been thinking of other ways. At its “mega site” in Varde, Denmark, with an initial capacity of 250MW, as well as district heating the plan is to channel excess heat into a 20 ha complex of greenhouses. “That means that Denmark can be self-sufficient with tomatoes during the six months of winter,” says Kristinsson. In turn, that means fewer imported vegetables: “that also saves a lot of carbon footprint, creates local jobs, and increases energy efficiency.” In Rjukan, Norway, Green Mountain’s datacentre channels excess heat to the fish farm next door.
Could other countries replicate this model? Yes and no. For one thing, the AI “hyperscalers” – such as Google, Meta, Amazon Web Services and Microsoft – dwarf Europe in terms of demand. Currently Europe’s datacentre capacity is estimated to be between 15% and 25% of that of the US. In addition, the renewable energy infrastructure in countries like Sweden has taken decades to establish; it is difficult to see the US catching up quickly. Added to which, European countries are relatively strict, both in terms of building and environmental regulations, and in areas like data privacy and protection. Elon Musk would never get away with trucking in some gas generators without permission in Sweden. To many critics, tighter regulation is exactly what the US datacentre landscape is crying out for. In July 2025, the Trump administration announced its AI Action Plan, which dismantled environmental and planning protections and rejected “radical climate dogma” in order to win the AI race.
Having said that, the US is building big in Nordic countries, to service their European users. In Sweden, Meta is building a 723MW facility in Lulea, Canadian-American firm Brookfield is planning a 750MW datacentre in Strängnäs, and Google broke ground on a 150MW plant in Horndal this June. These companies profess to be adopting the Nordic model, including building their own renewable energy supplies, although last month, the Guardian reported that Google had illegally felled 250,000 trees in Muhos, in northern Finland, to clear a site for its datacentre, leaving a barren 330 ha landscape. Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, has apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted “on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time” and planned to plant trees across 130 hectares there. Contractors building Microsoft’s datacentre in Gävle, Sweden, have been accused of housing their mostly foreign workers in poor conditions and subjecting them to long hours. Microsoft said of its contractors and suppliers, it “set clear requirements on health and safety, working conditions, and the freedom of association and right to collective bargaining” and had “robust processes in place” to ensure contractors’ compliance with Microsoft’s human rights and fair labour policies. The community engagement has not gone so smoothly for Google in Sweden, either. In 2021, a local metal band, also named Horndal, released an album railing against Google’s imminent arrival, called Lake Drinker (sample lyrics: “The digital devil shivers of thirst … First you took our trees / Now you drink our lake”).
Both atNorth and EcoDataCenter avoid importing cheap foreign labour, they say, but Kristinsson acknowledges that opposition to datacentres in the region has been growing, largely fuelled by the backlash in the US: “It’s probably not as strong [here], but Nordics are early adopters of everything that is new. We adopt, also, the same TikTok propaganda that is showing now in the US.”
Wernvik is more measured: “The American companies and the hyperscalers are definitely needed in the ecosystem as well because they possess unique competitiveness and capabilities.”
Could Sweden become a victim of its own success? The prospect of more and more of these gigantic facilities eating up the landscape is pretty dystopian even in a large country like Sweden. Wernvik is not too worried, though: “Our core components into what we sell are land and power. It’s a very linear business in that way. It’s very hard to have exponential growth because we work with physical constraints.” Exactly how many datacentres the world needs is largely a question of demand: how much more AI we require, and how much the benefits offset the harms. That’s really a separate conversation, but at the very least, Sweden’s joined-up, long-term approach to tech, energy and communities shows that there are better and worse ways to build our digital future.

title: KKR and RWE are rich firms. Why do they need a UK state loan for their windfarms? | Nils Pratley
article_text:
“This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain,” declared the prime minister.
Andy Burnham is obviously correct that the two Vanguard windfarms off the coast of Norfolk are huge investments. Together, they require almost £13bn of debt financing. But he can’t claim they represent a fresh expression of confidence. The project has been on the runway since the German utility RWE, the developer, was awarded a contract to build the windfarms in January’s renewables auction.
Instead, the new news on Wednesday was how the project will be financed, which is where the story becomes interesting. On the equity front, RWE said it had sold a 50% share in the Vanguard schemes to KKR, the giant US private equity and infrastructure investor. On the debt side, £12.8bn has come from “a consortium of 35 international banks”, including £1bn from the UK’s own national wealth fund (NWF).
It is fair enough, one might say, for the NWF to get involved – directing capital to energy transition projects is, in part, what it was set up to do. But here’s another key aspect of its role: the state-backed body is not meant to be a substitute for private capital; instead, its funding is supposed to be “additional”, in the terminology, to ensure infrastructure is built that might not otherwise be.
Here is how the NWF describes the process: “For each investment we are considering, we test and assess the extent to which impact would not have materialised without us, so we are confident we are delivering financial and non-financial value that would not otherwise be achieved.”
So how does that work with the Vanguard windfarms? Would they have been scrapped if the NWF had not chipped in its £1bn? That seems highly unlikely.
Consider that RWE is one of Europe’s biggest electricity generators and that KKR is a giant among private equity houses. These rich firms are experienced at raising capital. Consider, too, that the main way in which offshore wind projects are de-risked for developers is the auction process that sets a guaranteed inflation-linked price for their electricity for 20 years. In this case, the price is £91.20 a megawatt hour (in 2024 money), or high by historic standards.
If the cost of borrowing has risen post-auction – and it has – that’s unfortunate for RWE and KKR. They might have to pay a bit more for their debt, or pony up more equity, both of which would depress their returns. But that is an everyday risk of commercial life. Why did the NWF, having stayed away from fixed offshore wind until now, think it had to join a lending syndicate on a project where it is a stretch to think its contribution was the make-or-break element?
The NWF’s argument is that its involvement “widens the pool of capital available to offshore wind developers and helps to meet unprecedented liquidity requirements after the success of AR7 [the last auction round]”. In other words, the sector will need so much capital over coming years that the state-backed lender needs to be on standby.
It’s a defence, but it will sound very appealing from the point of view of developers. They can bid for an index-linked contract that guarantees revenues for 20 years; then, if borrowing conditions are tight, they are invited to think that the state will lend a hand to try to ease funding pressures. No wonder KKR wanted in. The NWF, note, says it is lending at market rates. Even so, its definition of how it adds “additional” value seems to have become very stretched.
Many of the NWF’s other big loans, such as billions for Sizewell C and £599m for Rolls-Royce’s development of small modular reactors, are far easier to understand. Those projects genuinely might not have happened without state backing. The same applies to the myriad of its smaller investments in battery technology and so forth.
Offshore wind generation, by contrast, is an established market with an effective mechanism – the contract-for-difference – for incentivising developers. The NWF’s pot of capital is not bottomless. Better targets for loans right now might be anything to do with electrification, meaning the take-up of heat pumps and electric vehicles, or storage solutions. As half the energy world is pointing out, it is where the big decarbonisation gains are available.
A bit of state activism to accelerate energy transition is a good thing, many of us would say. But, as argued here previously, more scrutiny of that “additionality” principle is overdue. There is little point replicating what the private sector would do anyway. When a huge private equity firm, KKR, is getting a helping hand because funding conditions are a bit rough, it is fair to ask if the state is achieving the best bang for its finite buck.

title: Burnham lauds £12bn offshore wind investment as he prepares for climate summit
article_text:
Andy Burnham has hailed a record investment in offshore wind, as the government tries to repair its green credentials after approving the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea.
On Wednesday the government announced a £12bn investment from the German energy company RWE and the US private equity firm KKR, as the prime minister prepares to travel to the Cop31 climate crisis summit in Turkey.
The investment package, which will go towards the creation of the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore windfarms off the Norfolk coast, is a “vote of confidence for building in Britain”, he said.
“It is great news for bill payers because every turbine we put up is power under British control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world.
“With coastal communities from Scotland to East Anglia powering Britain’s future, the places that host this energy benefit from the jobs and opportunities that it brings.”
The offshore wind projects will also receive £1bn in funding from the state-owned national wealth fund.
The windfarms are set to be providing power by 2030, with construction set to begin early next year. The wind investment is “believed to be the biggest of its kind in UK history”, the government said.
RWE said the Vanguard project represents one of the UK’s largest offshore wind developments, generating about 2.8 gigawatts, enough to supply 3m homes.
It estimated that the construction of the windfarms will create and support 2,300 jobs each year through its supply chain. The windfarms are expected to create a further 100 long-term permanent jobs when they are operational.
The energy company SSE also announced on Wednesday that the latest phase of its major offshore windfarm, Berwick Bank B off the east coast of Scotland, would “support” 2,600 existing jobs.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said investment in offshore wind and clean power was “creating quality jobs and rebuilding industry, while delivering the clean power we need to lower bills and reach net zero”.
She added that Britain was “leading from the front as a renewable energy powerhouse”.
It comes as Burnham seeks to bolster his government’s under-fire green credentials at Cop31, where he is expected to give a speech on Thursday.
The prime minister has faced a backlash from Labour MPs and environmental campaigners over his government’s decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield.
On Tuesday, ministers also rejected plans to build what would have been Britain’s biggest solar plant near the Blenheim Palace estate.
Fahnbulleh turned down the £800m Botley West project, which would have covered almost 3,500 acres of land. Developers said it would have provided enough electricity to power 330,000 homes.
Margaret Curran, in a letter on behalf of the energy secretary, wrote that the project would cause “substantial harm” to the green belt and the Blenheim Estate – home to Blenheim Palace, which is a world heritage site and the birthplace of Winston Churchill.

title: US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry
article_text:
China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.
As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.
Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.
Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.
“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”
For autocratic states without free and fair elections, seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added.
“They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”
He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”
China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.
Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way: “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”
China as a ‘doer and go-getter’
The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows.
Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.
The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue.
“Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”
Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed.
Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.
The need for trust
China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.
Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”
If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.
Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.
They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.
For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … so no major drama.”

title: Slight fall in carbon emissions from fossil fuels as Iran war drives renewables push
article_text:
Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.
Carbon dioxide from oil, gas and coal is forecast to flatline for 2026, based on data from the year so far, according to a comprehensive assessment by scientists. Emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% as drivers economise on fuel use and flock to electric vehicles instead.
The findings, presented on Tuesday morning at the Cop31 climate talks hosted by Turkey in Antalya, show both the impact of the Iran war and the global expansion of cheap renewable energy, chiefly solar and wind power.
Talk of a global turnaround would be premature, however, the report’s authors and other analysts said. The report was published in Nature Climate Change. The reduction in emissions from fossil fuels for 2026 will be about 0.4% compared with last year.
Yet this year’s slight fall could be temporary, and was more than offset by increased emissions from deforestation and land use change, following major fires in south-east Asia and further conversions of wild land to agriculture.
Many factors could disrupt the fragile trend of slowing emissions from fossil fuels, including an intensified expansion of coal in India, an easing of oil prices and US president Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for fossil fuels. Much greater investment in renewable energy, and low-carbon technology such as electric vehicles, would still be required to make permanent reductions in annual emissions, the report’s authors said.
Glen Peters, research professor at the Cicero Centre for International Climate Research, said: “A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak, unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions.”
About 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 will be emitted this year, according to the Global Carbon Budget, an annual assessment by scientists from scores of universities and science institutions around the world, published in the journal Earth System Science Data.
Energy demand continues to increase around the world, as more people gain access to electricity and are pulled out of poverty, but two-thirds of the increase is being met from rising generation from the sun and wind and the uptake of electric vehicles.
On the downside, emissions from deforestation and the conversion of land to agriculture have also ticked upward this year, leading to total carbon emissions rising slightly for the year, from 42.8bn tonnes last year to 43.3bn forecast for 2026.
The scientists warned that the world’s remaining “carbon budget” – the amount of carbon that can be poured into the atmosphere before global heating is likely to permanently exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels – was about 150bn tonnes, or less than four years at current rates.
Already, temperatures have exceeded the 1.5C threshold for more than two years, and El Niño conditions are heating the sea and air further. Global emissions must peak imminently and fall rapidly in subsequent years if the world is to have a chance of limiting the “overshoot” of temperatures above 1.5C.
China, the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases, is likely to reduce its carbon output by close to 1% this year, mostly because of a 5% reduction in oil use, following the Iran war. Peters said: “China has had flat emissions for the last few years after a fairly steep increase in the last decade. There’s been a lot of discussion about whether China has peaked or not. Whether this is just a one-off and China rebounds next year, we’ll have to wait and see, it’s too early to say.”
India’s emissions have grown strongly, mostly from an increase in coal use, while the country’s oil use has declined slightly. Emissions from the US are likely to fall by about 1.3% this year, as less coal is used, despite Trump’s attempts to boost it.
Bill Hare, chief executive of Climate Analytics, who was not involved in the research, cautioned against taking too much from the report. “The picture from the Global Carbon Budget is a flatline, not a decline – a projected fall of just 0.4% in 2026, a figure that is unfortunately statistically indistinguishable from zero,” he said. “We are heading towards a sustained breach of 1.5C by around 2030. With imminent overshoot, we are entitled to expect governments everywhere to move decisively to cut fossil fuel CO2 emissions.”
There seemed little sign of such a decisive move at Cop31, where more than 90 heads of state and government, and high-level representatives from more than 190 countries are gathering for a fortnight of talks on the climate crisis.
Hare said: “We see governments in countries such as Canada, the US and New Zealand rolling back climate policies as fast as they can, and countries such as Australia – co-president of Cop31 – continuing to press forward with massive coal and gas developments that are holding fossil fuel CO2 emissions at record levels. There is little sign yet that the Turkish and Australian leadership [of Cop31] intends to build on [the commitment to transition away from fossil fuels made three years ago] with stronger action.”

title: Senate advances bill to speed up projects from gas pipelines to clean energy
article_text:
The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.
It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America – everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. That is why climate advocates are torn over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs act (Baaja).
The Senate voted on Monday to open debate on Baaja in the first of several procedural votes. Senators voted 73-25 on the cloture motion, which did not result in the bill being passed, but pushed it another step forward.
Trump urged all senators to vote for the 417-page bill, which is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats in the Senate, but after last week’s historic “blue wave” elections, some environmental and tribal advocates called on Democratic leadership to pump the brakes.
Earthjustice, the Sierra Club and the ACLU have come out against the bill because it would significantly weaken environmental laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (Nepa) and accelerate the construction of gas pipelines and ICE detention centers.
Indigenous groups held a press conference on Friday calling on senators to vote against Baaja because it would weaken the federal government’s legal obligation to consult tribes on projects that affect them.
“This is such an existential threat to Indian country,” said Mark Macarro, president of the National Congress of American Indians.
Protesters rallied outside Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer’s building on Friday over concerns that the bill could boost datacenters. “It would be highly ironic if, having won an election where datacenter opposition was at the front and center, the first act of Congress was to make it easier to build datacenters,” said Bill McKibben.
Democrats elected in the blue wave will not take their seats until January, so the bill’s proponents still have time to rush it through the Senate, and technically there is time for it to pass in the House before new Congress and go to Trump.
But midterm success for the Democrats is dialing up the political friction. House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be the House speaker in the new Congress, said the bill “falls short in several areas”, including failing to protect tribal sovereignty, and he would not “rubber-stamp legislation without more constructive involvement with our caucus”.
Earlier on Monday, the bill’s Democratic sponsors, Senators Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse, said they had the votes to pass the bill. Heinrich said they had made last-minute changes to ensure tribal consultation, and they believed the bill would favor renewables over fossil fuels. “If we can create an open, competitive level playing field, clean is cheap, and cheap wins in the marketplace,” Heinrich said.
Whitehouse, who wore a tie with wind turbines on it, argued that passing the bill would set the stage for Democrats to work on clean energy policies next year with majorities in the House and Senate. “People should just cool their jets and have a little faith that this is not the end of the story,” he said.
Proponents of Baaja say it is needed because it takes too long to build large projects in America and the bill shortens timelines. It simplifies federal rules for building interstate transmission lines, it narrows what gets reviewed under the National Historic Preservation Act and limits tribal consultation, it limits the use of the Clean Water Act, shortens timelines for the Endangered Species Act, limits how the executive branch can interfere with federal permitting, and makes big changes to Nepa such as changing what requires Nepa review and who has standing to sue.
Baaja would expand fossil fuels
The fossil fuel industry is backing Baaja. The American Petroleum Institute (API) hailed the bill as “a historic opportunity” and called on congress to “finish permitting reform this year”.
“It creates a very accelerated fast track for gas pipelines,” said Earthjustice Action’s president, Abbie Dillen. “The gas industry is extraordinarily excited about this because they are interested in expanding existing pipeline capacity to get more liquefied natural gas out for export, and to be feeding power-hungry datacenters with gas.”
The bill could help pave the way for the Constitution gas pipeline that Williams Companies is trying to build through New York. The state denied the project’s water quality permit in 2016, but the company has revived the project under the Trump administration. The proposed pipeline could benefit from the bill’s changes to the Clean Water Act.
Baaja could also enable construction of gas pipelines in the west. Fossil fuel advocacy group Western States and Tribal Nations wants to build gas pipelines to feed domestic datacenters and export LNG from the west coast. During a 3 November election day meeting with Wyoming’s Sweetwater county board of commissioners, the advocacy group’s president, Andrew Browning, said he was talking to lawmakers about the bill: “The permitting bill’s a huge thing … We’re going to need that for everything we’re envisioning and building out.”
How the bill would increase clean energy
Some clean energy advocates want the bill to pass because it would connect renewables to the grid. Wind, solar and battery storage are now cheap to build, but the country lacks the necessary transmission lines to bring clean energy where it’s needed.
Interstate transmission lines can take a decade to get built, and energy projects also face a bottleneck in connecting to the grid. At the end of 2025, 2,060 GW of total generation and storage capacity were waiting in a queue to connect to the grid.
Ben King, energy and climate director at Rhodium Group, said Baaja would reform the interconnection queue process and unlock the ability to build the transmission that is needed. “We’re at a pretty low point for policy support for clean [energy],” he said, referring to Trump’s repeal of clean energy tax credits. “[Baaja] sets up the ability to build stuff more quickly for when the next wave of climate policy happens.”
Many experts have modeled what the bill would do to emissions, but there is a lot of uncertainty on that question. Rhodium Group’s analysis found that domestic emissions go down if Baaja passes. But another model by the Purdue engineering professor Kevin Kircher found it would increase domestic emissions.
Kircher said the optimistic case for Baaja is that there’s a huge amount of clean energy ready to go, and if we get rid of the long queues and regulations, “level the playing field and let it rip”, then clean energy wins on the economics. “I think that understanding is outdated,” he said.
What the bill does to emissions partly depends on what type of energy gets connected to the grid. Rhodium Group assumed, based on a report from 2025, that 85% of the capacity added to the grid would be renewables. But Kircher said some grid operators have updated their queues this year to remove redundant and speculative offers. (PJM’s queue as of 3 August looks quite gassy.)
King said the economics show an impressive decrease in the cost of renewables, while fossil fuels are not getting any cheaper. “Some of it is just a bet on what’s going to win out in the future,” he said. “Our modeling suggests that clean stuff is going to dominate energy expansion for the foreseeable future, and there might be people who have a different view on that. API might have a different perspective – they might bet that there’s more room for them to grow.”
Kircher emphasized that the various models have not had time for peer review since the bill was first introduced on 30 September. “We need to have some humility in recognizing that the process of taking that 417 pages of super dense legal text and mapping it … is extremely complicated and full of uncertainties,” he said.
What the bill would do to Nepa
The bill would significantly reduce the scope of Nepa. It would narrow the definition of a “major federal action” that would trigger Nepa review, and effectively eliminate the authority of courts to enforce Nepa compliance.
Nepa is the powerful law that attorneys used to block the Trump administration’s plans to convert 11 mega-warehouses into massive ICE detention centers. If the bill passes, it could accelerate the development of ICE detention centers, according to a letter the American Civil Liberties Union sent to senators. “As written, this bill would hamper, if not altogether thwart, critical work by the ACLU and our partners to halt ICE’s dangerous expansion of immigrant detention,” the letter said.
Baaja’s passage would be “the single biggest overhaul” of American environmental laws since the 1970s, said Dillen of Earthjustice. “There are legitimate concerns that Nepa has been weaponized to slow down important projects, but people have recognized this problem for years, and the law has been reformed, and it’s also been weakened very significantly by the supreme court. What this bill does is take the last pieces of it that are very relevant in an administration like this,” she said.
Trump has pushed a “drill, baby, drill” fossil fuel agenda, and Baaja’s weakening of environmental regulations would further embolden him, Dillen said. She pointed to Trump’s plan to allow drilling near Chaco Culture national historic park, a Unesco world heritage site. “Chaco Canyon is in the crosshairs,” she said.
“At Earthjustice, we are deeply committed to building clean energy and to do it in a time frame that is meaningful, given the threats that we face. But the way to do this, the way to build our country better and even faster, is not by running over tribes and by emboldening a president who voters have just come out in a historic turnout to push back on,” Dillen said.

title: High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate chief tells Cop31
article_text:
A global fossil fuel price crisis is “spreading inflation like a cancer” around the planet, the UN’s climate chief, Simon Stiell, told the opening plenary of critical UN climate talks in Turkey.
Stiell joined Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia, which is leading the negotiations, in promoting renewable energy and a new electrification goal as an optimistic alternative to a planet still tied to oil, coal and gas.
Inside the tight security of the opening plenary on Monday, delegates from almost 200 countries watched a stirring short film with scenes of fire, flood and storms that proclaimed: “It’s time to reconnect with the planet we have grown apart from.”
