Turkey said it expected 100,000 visitors, including national delegations, to attend the two-week talks, including at least 95 heads of state. A global leaders summit is scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday. But the talks are under increased pressure to deliver, after growing dissatisfaction with the snail’s pace of results.
The talks are opening as a historic El Niño builds in the tropical Pacific and months after a glacier collapse set off catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet, wiping away villages and killing at least 1,459 people, with thousands more still missing. Climate scientists confirmed this year that global heating would reach at least 1.8C – beyond the 1.5C temperature goal that countries promised to aim for at talks in Paris in 2015.
Last week Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, told the Guardian that although he still had faith in the negotiating process, “the fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast … and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”
And in a statement the UN secretary general, António Guterres, urged leaders to “get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need”.
Stiell also said: “The urgency of this moment must drive us forward. Global heating is already costing the Earth,” adding that it was vulnerable communities paying the price and frustration at a lack of fairness was palpable.
US president Donald Trump’s war with Iran and the disruption of the key strait of Hormuz supply route for oil pushed up petrol prices around the world by 50%, raising inflation and slowing economic growth.
Stiell told delegates this “fossil fuel cost chaos” had “delivered a global shock wave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer”.
Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, the president of the negotiations, said in a speech that will set the tone for the talks that although the 1.5C Paris target will be overshot “we can return … if we work together and act with urgency, solidarity and resolve”.
With fists clenched in the final moments of a speech, Bowen urged delegates to show future generations that this generation was “equal to the challenge” and to “rise to this moment together”.
The countries pushing for the greatest action at Cop31 have stressed the 1.5C temperature rise limit can’t be abandoned and called for accelerated steps to provide finance to the places most vulnerable to climate impacts. The so-called high-ambition coalition said it has 20 country members pushing for major progress in Antalya.
 
“That limit is in serious danger but overshoot should never become an excuse for inaction, every fraction of a degree matters,” said Jess Gasper, environment minister for the Marshall Islands.
“We must limit overshoot and return to a safe temperature as quickly as possible.”
 
Gasper said it took eight years to get international finance to build a single sea wall to help protect the Marshall Islands, a Pacific island nation acutely threatened by sea level rise.
“That example shows we need that money to adapt,” he said. “I refuse to accept that we experience displacement because the world fails to act.”
The talks began without a fight over the agenda, which was considered by many to be a good sign. There was confidence among delegates that a final decision from Cop31 would include reference to a new voluntary electrification goal being championed by the host, Turkey, and the president of the negotiations, Australia.
Bowen said he had spoken to countries around the globe that were represented at the talks and there was “enormous momentum” among them for electrification.
The goal, he said, was to raise the percentage of final energy consumption coming from electricity from the current one-fifth to one-third in the next ten years.
Dr Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency, said: “I have talked with many governments and I see there is a great appetite for many countries to be part of this historic decision [in Antalya].”
He told the Guardian: “The important thing is that we are entering the age of electricity and this [electrification goal] would give an extra boost to that movement.”
Countries agreed at the 2023 climate summit to triple renewable energy capacity by 2030. Birol said if countries endorsed the 2035 electrification target it would give an “unmistakable signal to markets” and a chance to increase both renewable and nuclear electricity.

title: There’s more than a whiff of politics to the sudden call to slash Labor’s green energy subsidies
article_text:
As Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, comes under increasing pressure to fight inflation by slashing spending in the midyear budget update, the drumbeat is loudest for cuts in one specific area: green energy subsidies for households.
Receiving the most focus is the cheaper home batteries program, which from July last year has offered a taxpayer-backed 30% rebate to households and businesses.
The scheme has become a victim of its own success. Treasury officials originally estimated it would lead to a million new batteries by 2030 at a cost of $2.3bn. The latest estimate is more than triple that figure, and only after a tweak to the policy.
Also in the crosshairs is the 2022 electric vehicle subsidy, which exempts workers from fringe benefits tax when they lease an EV through their employer and has proved more popular – and expensive – than predicted.
Despite reports that Treasury is pushing for cuts to the home battery scheme, the argument has hardly been made.
There is more than a whiff of politics to the sudden and urgent need to do away with clean energy programs, against, say, scaling back billions of dollars in diesel fuel rebates for miners.
When budget experts are asked broader questions about the big pressures on the federal government’s finances, rarely do they cite handouts for home batteries or tax breaks for electric vehicles.
In a speech on Monday, Angus Taylor, the opposition leader, again promised to “abolish Labor’s ideological climate bureaucracy” as part of his promised $31bn of budget savings over four years.
Meanwhile, the Albanese government’s recent efforts to apply an income test to private healthcare rebates for over-65s was met with howls of protest from the Coalition.
As Stephen Bartos, an economics professor at the University of Canberra, says, in all this talk about cutting spending “nobody is mentioning nuclear-powered submarines”.
Bartos, a former deputy secretary at the Department of Finance and New South Wales parliamentary budget officer, says if the challenge is to close the budget deficit then green subsidies “shouldn’t be their first port of call”.
“Partly because it’s small beer compared to the big-ticket items like health, NDIS and defence. But also because there is a rationale for green subsidies, if a declining one.”
The national disability insurance scheme, for example, was expected to cost nearly $54bn in 2025–26, which has made reining in the cost of the scheme an existential question for the government’s fiscal plans. In 2023, the Parliamentary Budget Office estimated the total cost of acquiring nuclear-powered submarines under the Aukus agreement to be as much $368bn over the life of the program.
The federal fuel tax credit scheme, which mainly helps major global mining companies, costs about $11bn a year and is rising fast.
Bartos is critical of government tax breaks for electric vehicles but says the case for public support for batteries is stronger.
“I would probably be looking at where the price signals encouraging adoption [of clean energy] are weakest, and that’s probably batteries. For EVs, people are shifting no matter what.”
The case for the cheaper batteries scheme has also been undermined by Treasury officials’ abject failure to predict how popular it would be. A month into the program and it was already obvious they had got it wrong, as the expected cost blew out towards $14bn.
Not only was our appetite for subsidised batteries way higher than official forecasts, the original design of the scheme made it more desirable to buy bigger, more expensive batteries.
There has since been a tweak to the design to account for that second issue, which is how Treasury now predicts – for what it’s worth – that the program will cost $7.2bn.
These cost blowouts have amplified derision of the home batteries as “middle-class welfare” of the worst sort.
Alison Reeve, the director of the energy and climate change program at the Grattan Institute, understands the concerns but says the evidence to back that claim “is pretty thin when you look at where the batteries are being installed”.
Notably, this is in homes across outer suburbia, such as western Sydney, and in regional areas. In other words, not in enclaves of the comfortably well-off.
Then there is the bigger-picture issue: that we risk sacrificing long-term clean energy goals in the name of short-term fiscal objectives.
“Batteries are going to be a big part of our energy future,” Reeve says. “We do need to do some stimulating of that industry until it can stand on its own two feet.”
Slashing support for batteries would damage the burgeoning web of small businesses, suppliers and tradies who have invested in servicing the infant batteries industry.
That is not to say there are ways to improve the cost and benefits trade-off in the home batteries program. This could be by ensuring subsidised batteries deliver a community benefit by contributing to the power grid in times of need.
“We need to make sure we are maximising the public benefit, rather than just the private benefit,” Reeve says.
There are lessons in how Western Australia has designed its home batteries support scheme.
“If you look at the west coast, you couldn’t get the state subsidy unless you linked yourself up to a virtual power plan run by the network operator. That was in order to benefit the whole network,” she says.
“We also need a clear path out of the subsidy so it doesn’t grow uncontrollably.”

title: UK households face rush to find green energy installer to beat April VAT hike
article_text:
Households planning to invest in green energy upgrades, including heat pumps and solar panels, risk a nationwide rush to find an installer or face hundreds of pounds in unexpected costs unless the government abandons its looming VAT increase.
Ministers are under growing pressure to reverse plans to scrap the 5% VAT exemption on home heat pumps, solar panels and batteries from 1 April which could add up to £1,530 on to the cost of a smart home energy system amid record demand for fossil fuel alternatives.
Industry groups have warned that the VAT cliff-edge could trigger a surge in demand for installations before the deadline, creating a “feast and famine” upheaval for the country’s nascent network of home energy installers after years of tepid interest from households.
Demand for home energy upgrades has reached record highs across the UK since the Middle East war caused gas market prices to double across Europe, pushing home energy bills to near four-year highs.
But the chancellor’s budget statement has signalled plans to shrink the total amount for heat pump grants over the coming financial year, while cutting the extra grant funding offered to heating oil users at the same time as VAT is reinstated.
Charlotte Lee, the chief executive of Heat Pump Association UK, said the abrupt change risks “creating a rush of applications ahead of April, disrupting the supply chain and making the process less predictable for consumers.
“The savings to government must be weighed against the risk of disrupting consumers, undermining industry confidence and stalling an emerging market,” she said.
The trade association is seeking clarity from the government over how the reintroduction of VAT will be applied so households can avoid an unexpected bill if their pre-booked installation is delayed until after the VAT exemption deadline.
Meanwhile, the decision to remove the VAT relief has been criticised as “inconsistent” with the government’s focus on helping to protect bill payers from the surging cost of fossil fuels, and “total policy madness” after ministers cut VAT on electricity bills in part to encourage electric alternatives to fossil fuels.
The Liberal Democrats said the rollback of the tax exemption could mean a household planning to fit an air-source heat pump, a 4KW solar installation, and a home battery would face an extra £1,530 cost unless it is able to undertake the work before April.
Pippa Heylings, the Liberal Democrat’s spokesperson for Energy Security and Net Zero, said: “It is total policy madness for the government to strip VAT from electricity bills with one hand, only to slap it straight back on to heat pumps with the other. They are telling families to switch to clean electricity, while simultaneously punishing them with a £1,530 tax hike for buying the very kit needed to do so.”
Heylings called on ministers to “urgently reverse this shortsighted heat pump tax”, a demand echoed by energy industry leaders who fear the rise may undermine government schemes to support the industry, which includes the launch of state-backed low-interest loans.
Chris Hewett, the chief executive of Solar Energy UK, said the rise would “raise the cost of the loans scheme that has only just been launched” and would be “inconsistent with the government’s intention for more people to enjoy the benefits of home solar and battery systems”.
“With domestic electricity bills now zero-rated until July next year, saving energy will be taxed more heavily than consuming it – a perverse incentive. We will be urging the government to reverse course,” he said.
A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson said: “More and more families are switching to clean energy technology, with record numbers of people applying for heat pumps and receiving grants through the Boiler Upgrade Scheme in September.
“We are driving forward electrification and the clean tech market, protecting support for low-income families and launching our new warm homes loan scheme so households can purchase heat pumps, solar panels and batteries at no upfront cost.”

title: Rare call for more electricity supplies as wind power drops across Europe
article_text:
The government body tasked with keeping the lights on issued a rare call for more electricity supplies on Monday morning due to low wind power generation forecasts across Europe.
A notice issued by the National Energy System Operator (Neso) on Sunday night said it faced a “shortfall” of almost 1,400 megawatts in its electricity supply margins from 6am until 11am on Monday.
The notice said Neso would need to find extra generation of about 800 megawatts, or the equivalent of a medium-sized gas power plant, within eight hours before a review of power supplies scheduled for 4am.
A second “electricity margin notice” issued after the pre-dawn review revealed that Neso’s 11th-hour margin call helped to shrink its shortfall to 500MW. It said that no further contingency power was required but Neso could still call on power plants to generate more than usual between 8am and 11am.
A later update said the shortfall had shrunk again, to 200MW, before being cancelled entirely just after 9am.
In the past, these notices would typically have been used during cold, winter evenings, when electricity use is often at its highest for the year, to call for extra power supplies to meet the peak in demand.
The unusual morning power shortfall has followed an uptick in Neso alerts over recent months, including the first margin notices to be issued during this summer when heatwaves pushed demand higher while curbing generation.
A spokesperson for Neso, which balances the power system’s supply and demand on a minute-by-minute basis around the clock, said the notice was “a routine and precautionary measure” to give the market “an opportunity” to make extra generation capacity available.
“This is not a warning of power cuts, there is no risk to customer electricity supplies, and customers do not need to take action – Great Britain’s electricity system remains secure,” the spokesperson said.
The market notice was issued despite there being no constraints within the electricity grid which might make power plants or windfarms unavailable, and while the UK is forecast to export electricity to Europe.
This suggests that the shortfall may have been prompted by low wind speeds across Europe, which have curbed the continent’s renewable energy output at the end of last week.
In northern Europe, periods with a reduction in solar and wind power are referred to as Dunkelflaute, German for “dark doldrums”, in the renewable energy sector.
On Friday, Neso paid more than 10 times the market price of earlier in the week to secure power imports from Europe, which will ultimately be covered through charges on home energy bills.
Kathryn Porter, an independent energy consultant, said these payments included £2,500 a megawatt-hour for power imported via Great Britain’s high voltage subsea cables, and £1,000/MWh to fire up gas plants.
The system operator is under scrutiny after an independent investigation, published last month, found significant and concerning “cultural issues” within the grid operator’s control room.
The three-month investigation was undertaken by an external law firm after whistleblowers accused Neso of covering up the growing risk of blackouts faced by the country.
After a string of margin notices over the summer, the whistleblowers claimed the grid was becoming increasingly unmanageable, and that control room decisions were subject to “interference” by the company’s corporate affairs team to protect the reputation of the government-owned operator.
Neso was once part of the FTSE 100 energy company National Grid. It came back under government control in 2024.
Separately on Monday, benchmark Dutch and British wholesale gas prices rose amid colder weather forecasts, increasing demand for heating.
The benchmark Dutch month-ahead contract edged up by €0.91 to €86.50 (£72) a MWh, ICE data showed. The equivalent British contract rose by 2.75 pence to 215p a therm.
Wholesale energy prices remain in focus as markets closely watch developments in the Middle East conflict.
The LSEG gas analyst Yuriy Onyshkiv said: “News is mixed. Trump downplayed the likelihood of further US strikes on Iran while talks progress, which eases geopolitical risk. However, both sides reported shipping hit in or near the strait of Hormuz.
The US president, Donald Trump, said on Sunday he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progressed. The Brent crude oil price fell 0.6% to just under $96 (£72)a barrel on Monday.
The AA said petrol prices had peaked at 174.7p a litre earlier this month to reach their highest since August 2022 but started this week at 169.7p.

title: Who’s who at Cop31: key players at the climate talks
article_text:
Australia
Hosting Cop was a key pledge from Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese in 2021, while in opposition, before his successful election campaign. But arcane rules meant the country had to wait its turn to bid and was then embroiled in an angry row with Turkey over the hosting. The final compromise put Australia in charge of the negotiations which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya. The bitter taste left by the row lingers and Australia has seemed to some a rather half-hearted host. The country’s media has been much quieter on Cop than previous host countries, and although Albanese will speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment, he is unlikely to stay long.
Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, will be in daily charge of the negotiations. As aspects of Australia’s energy supply also fall under his portfolio, he has been in the sometimes uncomfortable position of having to boost fossil fuels while insisting on the need for a clean energy transition.
Yet Australia has a positive story to tell on decarbonisation: while remaining one of the world’s major fossil fuel exporters, the country has also invested heavily in renewables, and solar power has now expanded so much that consumers are sometimes offered free electricity.
Turkey
Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Turkey’s autocratic president, showed little interest in climate and environmental concerns before bidding to host this year’s Cop summit.
In the last five years, Cop has also been held in Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Azerbaijan, all in the same broad region. This has given an outsize role to the Arab group of countries, who are neighbours in the region and have a strong interest in ensuring that fossil fuel interests – including their lobbyists – are well represented.
Australia runs the overall direction of the negotiations, and Turkey’s government, with the environment minister, Murat Kurum, has control of the action agenda, a programme of voluntary initiatives. Erdoğan has used this to push forward a key interest of his wife, Emine Erdoğan, in cutting waste and promoting the circular economy. She has called for an end to “throwaway culture” and for recycling instead of landfill – though Turkey still has sites that leak vast quantities of methane.
Fatih Birol, the head of the International Energy Agency and one of the world’s leading energy economists, is understood to be one of the advisers behind this year’s emphasis on electrification, displacing fossil fuels with electricity for heating, transport and industrial uses. This could halve the amount of energy we need, and is the next biggest step, after boosting renewable energy generation, needed for a low-carbon world.
Brazil
The recently re-elected President Lula da Silva will come to Cop31 for his first trip abroad after winning his historic fourth term, and will bring two roadmaps, one a global plan for the transition away from fossil fuels, the other for halting and reversing deforestation. These are non-binding, and contain no deadlines or firm requirements from governments, but show a series of steps that governments can take to achieve these goals.
China
Xi Jinping, the president of China, will not come to this year’s Cop, but his country’s rapid energy and industrial transformation will determine the course of the planet’s future. China is the world’s second biggest economy and the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases, making up nearly a third of global annual carbon output, owing mainly to the use of fossil fuels to power its explosive economic growth for the last 25 years. But it has also invested in renewable energy, which is reshaping the global energy business.
Xi may not be present in Antalya, but the top officials he sends will know that petrostates – including Russia, Saudi Arabia and the UAE – are his important allies. However, countries pushing for a low-carbon future may be more important still – as China’s customers.
India
For several months this year, India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, mulled an intriguing proposition: to host the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028. In the end, India withdrew its bid in April without specifying why, leaving the field open. India is torn between its burgeoning clean energy sector – it now has the world’s third biggest installed capacity of renewable energy, after China and the US – and its coal sector, which still supplies about 70% of electricity, and has close links to Modi.
Bhupender Yadav, India’s environment minister, who leads its Cop delegations, enjoys a mutually supportive relationship with the UK’s Ed Miliband, and a reputation as a forward thinker.
US
The attention of Donald Trump has been fixed on the crucial midterm elections, a verdict on his second term as president that has shown Republicans the electoral dangers of an unpredictable White House. No US delegation is expected at Cop31, and soon Trump’s withdrawal of the country from the UN framework convention on climate change will mean none can take part.
Trump’s shadow was felt at Cop30 in Belem last year, as he started to dismantle the US’s renewable energy sector and boost fossil fuels, setting the US on course to start increasing greenhouse gas emissions again, after decades in which they fell. But his administration’s unpopularity with the US electorate, and a drought and fire-filled summer, has bolstered the pro-climate stance of scores of Democratic congresspeople and state governors, despite a campaign of “climate hushing” before the midterms. Some of them, and a scattering of business leaders, may attend Cop31.
UK
Andy Burnham will attend Cop for the first time this year, after a mixed record on the climate since taking office. During the record-breaking heatwaves and droughts of this summer, the British prime minister was criticised for failing to speak out on the climate crisis. He subsequently made strong interventions affirming his support for the UK’s target of reaching net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, but then backed the Jackdaw gasfield. No decision has been announced on the Rosebank oilfield yet.
From December, Burnham will have a much bigger opportunity to craft climate policy on the international stage: the UK will take over the revolving presidency of the influential G20 group, which comprises the world’s biggest developed and developing economies. The Guardian understands that the UK will emphasise building resilience against the impacts of the climate crisis as a key focus of the G20 for its year-long presidency.
Miliband, now foreign secretary, and a veteran of many Cops in government and opposition, is expected to accompany the prime minister to the leaders’ summit segment of Cop31. Miliband was hailed, in public and private, by many participants last year for his patient bridge-building that helped Brazil to rescue a deal from the fractious final hours of Cop30.
At this year’s UN general assembly, he also briefed other governments on the findings of the UK’s joint intelligence committee, which warned that the impact of collapsing ecosystems around the world posed a national security risk, threatening food shortages, mass migration and potential nuclear war.
The energy and net zero secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, will head the UK’s Cop31 delegation for the final negotiations in the last days of this fortnight of talks, after the leaders have departed.
Europe
The EU has faced a quandary over its climate convictions in recent years. Far-right populists are on the rise, pushing climate denialism, and the bloc has backed down from some key regulations, watering down its green deal package, loosening the strings on corporate climate liabilities, delaying rules on trade in goods from deforested areas, and extending the phase-in of new car rules. The failure of Europe’s car industry to move decisively to electric vehicles – preferring lobbying against emissions standards, which has turned out to be a poor strategy as consumers turn in droves to cheap-to-run EVs – has led to threats to slap tariffs on China.
The EU commission president, Ursula von der Leyen called this summer’s record-breaking heatwaves and drought a “summer of truth” that must be answered: she is now confirmed for the summit. Wopke Hoekstra, the Dutch climate commissioner, will oversee the final stages of the talks for the EU, and is expected to make competition with China a key focus.
UN
Cop31 will mark the final outing at a UN climate summit for António Guterres, the UN secretary general, who has regularly intervened powerfully on this subject. A successor to Guterres has still not yet been chosen – the US has tried to get Viktor Orbán, the far-right former president of Hungary, into the role, or a former minister from the United Arab Emirates, Lana Nusseibeh.
Simon Stiell, the determined executive secretary of the UNFCCC, will oversee the talks, with an added twist to his job this year, having to liaise between the two co-hosts as well as the fractious parties.
Saudi Arabia
Saudi failed to confirm with the Guardian before Cop who would lead its delegation, but the country’s recent behaviour at international climate meetings tells its own story. The country has a long history of obstructing the UN climate negotiations, though its behaviour was sometimes muted when the US intervened. With Trump in the White House, Saudi has felt emboldened to interfere further, with allies including Russia, Venezuela, members of the Arab group, and the Like-Minded Developing Countries grouping.
At Cop30, the Saudi delegation refused to allow even an oblique mention of the pledge to “transition away from fossil fuels”, made at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, in the final text until the final moments.
At recent meetings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Saudi led a small group of countries – including China, India, Russia and Kenya – that fought to delay publication of the next comprehensive assessment of climate science. Publication of the landmark report, which is expected to warn of catastrophic impacts from further temperature rises, was expected in 2028, in time for Cop33 at which countries will assess their progress on meeting emissions-cutting goals under the Paris agreement, a process known as the “global stocktake”. Delaying it by a year or more, as Saudi wants, would mean a loss of urgency for the global stocktake, and could help countries to get away with inadequate measures on decarbonisation.

title: Lanarkshire AI datacentre to fully rely on national grid despite renewables claim
article_text:
A datacentre company that said it would power a massive AI development near Glasgow with renewable energy has admitted that the scheme will be entirely served by the national grid.
DataVita, a key plank of the UK’s AI strategy, had promised that the Lanarkshire project would draw 1GW – the equivalent output of a small nuclear reactor, or Britain’s largest windfarm – from green sources. But when the Guardian raised questions about the pledge, it said the arrangement was “subject to final commercial agreements, planning, grid and consenting processes”.
Now, the company, which says its proposals would transform the economy of the village of Chapelhall, outside Airdrie, has quietly revised the plan. It now says the datacentres will be “fully grid served” with the possibility that solar and windfarms “could connect in the future”.
DataVita says the power it draws from the grid will be largely renewable energy. The company remains in receipt of £202m of public money in the form of wealth guarantees from Britain’s national wealth fund.
While the shift may appear to have been inevitable given the implausibility of the claimed renewables provision, it could present a problem for both DataVita and Britain’s AI strategy.
Under the former prime minister Keir Starmer, Britain’s AI strategy was to build massive datacentres in zones across the country. Their developers would get incentives – including, potentially, discounts on energy and expedited planning approvals. DataVita was to build one of the key developments associated with this strategy, an “AI growth zone” in Lanarkshire.
But this strategy began to founder just over a year after it was announced, when the Guardian’s investigations demonstrated that there was little solidity behind many announced plans.
AI datacentres are some of the most energy-intensive structures humanity has ever built, and energy costs are higher in Britain than in most of Europe. There is a years-long wait for the UK developments to connect to the grid.
Two key UK AI investments – announced with great fanfare by Starmer’s government – are on shaky ground after questions emerged over their ability to power themselves, or pay the high energy costs necessary to realise their stated ambitions. Now DataVita, which was supposed to bring 3,400 jobs to Lanarkshire by building a 500MW datacentre, also appears to be backtracking on its energy plans.
In a response to the Guardian, the company said it had not misrepresented its intention to supply renewables to the site earlier this year. “Our commitment to renewable energy is unchanged,” said a spokesperson. However, they added: “Our datacentres are being designed to be grid served … Our grid supply will be through a renewable power purchase agreement.”
This appears to contradict an earlier announcement, in which the company said: “More than 1GW of renewable energy capacity, including wind, solar, and battery storage, will be delivered through private wire connections directly linked to the datacentres.”
DataVita left open the possibility that its datacentres would connect to renewable energy in the future, through a wind and solar park it proposes to build in North Lanarkshire.
Kat Jones, the director of the Edinburgh-based charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland, said DataVita’s apparent change in direction was “emblematic of the hyperbolic claims being made by datacentre developers in Scotland”.
“Hyperscale AI datacentres simply cannot run on renewable power alone, they absolutely need a highly reliable source of grid power,” she said. “It is not surprising that the goalposts have now changed.”

title: ‘Scapegoating’: green groups condemn plan to axe Environment Agency and Natural England
article_text:
Scientists have accused the government of scapegoating nature for proposing to scrap the only environmental regulator with a legal duty to protect the natural world.
Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, said on Monday that the independent regulator Natural England and the Environment Agency were being reviewed as part of a wider shake-up of quangos, or arm’s length bodies. Ministers are considering abolishing the two biggest environmental regulators in an attempt to give politicians greater control over what gets built and where.
But Haigh’s proposal appears to be in contradiction to previous policy which puts Natural England at the heart of planning changes to boost growth and build 1.5m new homes by the end of this parliament.
A coalition of leading environmental charities including the RSPB, Wildlife Trusts, National Trust and the British Trust for Ornithology criticised the abolition of Natural England as a costly mistake that would leave the country more exposed to fire, flood, drought and wildlife extinctions. “It would shake the credibility of any government claiming to care about our natural world,” the groups said in an open letter.
Announcing the proposals, Haigh repeated disputed allegations that nature and regulations to protect it were blocking development. She told business leaders: “Over decades, politicians were content to duck accountability by giving responsibility away from ministers to a sprawling web of regulators and arm’s length bodies, more than 20 statutory consultees, all with veto power, notionally bound by statutory deadlines. But obfuscation has become normal.
“As part of rewiring the state, we will reform arm’s length bodies to increase public control. We will look at each of their functions and pose the challenge: what should be devolved, what can be dissolved and what can be delivered by departments?
“We’ve already begun that process with the Environment Agency, Natural England, Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate.”
But the government’s own analysis shows there is little evidence that nature is a block to development.
Sally Hayns, the chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Ecology and Environmental Management, said: “Scapegoating nature, and those that work to protect it, won’t get Britain building.
“The government’s own impact assessments have found ‘very limited’ evidence that environmental protections hold back development. In fact nature is an essential resilience tool: making homes cooler in heatwaves, safer from flooding and surrounded by the green spaces people want to live near.”
Natural England has repeatedly been at the centre of culture wars, most recently when it was wrongly accused of planning a cull of Dartmoor ponies – a claim promoted by those on the political right.
The body is in charge of regulating and overseeing more than 5,000 of the most protected natural sites in England – home to some of the most threatened species, including nightingales, woodpeckers and long-eared owls. Its role is to advise on how proposed developments and local plans affect biodiversity, geodiversity, landscapes, seascapes, soils, access, and protected sites or species.
Tony Juniper, the chair of Natural England, said his organisation had helped speed up building by reviewing rules such as those that protect bats and newts. “A healthy natural environment is vital for economic development and at Natural England we are very proud of all the work we have done during recent years to unite our national ambitions for growth while achieving nature’s recovery,” Juniper said.
The legal duties of Natural England and the EA would still have to be enforced even if the bodies were abolished, critics said. Haigh has suggested ministers may take on these roles, or they could be devolved.
But the political control of such a significant environmental regulator was condemned by the environmental groups.
“Our rivers should be a cautionary tale,” they said. “Political interference in the business of regulation led to chronic underinvestment in water and sewerage infrastructure. Repeated ministerial authorisation to use toxic chemicals against independent advice led to years of contamination.”
Craig Bennett, the chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts, said: “For over 16 years, politicians have been claiming that the regulations and regulators who protect English wildlife are some sort of obstacle on a path to prosperity. They are not. For over 16 years, protections have been chipped away and the woods, meadows, skylarks and hares they protect are suffering a death by a thousand cuts.”
Many of the proposals Haigh announced are likely to follow the recommendations made in a report by Jon Cunliffe last year, who proposed replacing Ofwat with a new super-regulator that would take in powers from Natural England and the Environment Agency.
Natural England and the Environment Agency have faced criticism from environmentalists for being too weak after years of budget cuts.
But Richard Benwell, chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said: “The answer is to restore its effectiveness, not abolish it.
“Scrapping the regulator would be scapegoating, not reform. A government serious about growth and environmental security should welcome independent scrutiny, not fear it.”

title: The good news out of Cop31? That most of the world’s governments said no to an agreement stripped of meaning | Bill Hare
article_text:
The failure of Cop31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multilateralism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.
The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. What we also know is that co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia. It didn’t work.
Governments have spent the past 35 years negotiating the global response to preventing “dangerous interference” with the climate system. Over that same period global warming has increased to close to 1.4C, with observed warming now accelerating above 0.3C per decade. Now, we’re facing an imminent breach of the Paris agreement’s critical 1.5C warming limit.
Successive Australian governments have either actively denied the problem exists – or have talked loud and long about how they are playing their role.
And what a role it has been! Australia’s coal exports have tripled since 1991; LNG exports have increased 20-fold. Australia now contributes about 4.3% of global fossil carbon emissions through both its domestic activities, and as the third-largest exporter of fossil fuels of all time.
Now that Australia’s efforts to host successful climate talks have failed so badly to deliver at a global level, we must turn to the urgent question: what will the government deliver for Australians at home?
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has called the current decade “critical” for combating climate change. He told leaders at Cop31 they had a “solemn responsibility” to act – and he’s said that every fraction of a degree of warming prevented matters.
If anyone needed confirmation of that during the past year, they only needed to turn on the TV news or, in some cases, to walk out of their house. From Adelaide to Sydney, the south-east broiled in January. Bush burned, homes ignited, lungs filled with smoke. Can you guess what made the heat so brutal? And the floods so powerful?
Further afield, in countries that gave the Australian colony many of its people, things were equally desperate. Italy, Greece, Britain, Spain … all of Europe crackled through its summer, leaving an estimated 50,000 people dead before their time.
South and east Asia (many of them our LNG markets) shared the pain, with temperatures hitting a close-to-unliveable 52C in Pakistan. All of it driven by climate change; all of it driven by burning fossil fuels.
So that’s the logical framing when you hear government ministers from the prime minister down celebrating new fossil fuel finds, talking about how the country benefits from extracting and exporting coal, oil and gas.
What we’re exporting is climate pain.
The government clearly didn’t turn on the TV news nor leave its house this year: it was too busy planning for coal and gas exports staying close to present levels over the next decade, at exactly the time emissions globally should be halving.
In Australia’s approvals pipeline are four “carbon bombs”, defined by scientists as projects that could emit a billion or more tonnes of fossil CO2. Off the coast of Western Australia there’s the Browse gas development at the pristine Scott Reef, the Valhalla fracking project in WA’s Kimberley further north, the Beetaloo basin fracking project in the Northern Territory, and the massive Hunter Valley Operations coalmine in New South Wales.
Albanese’s ministers have shown little other than full-blooded support for these projects going ahead. Is it no wonder then that we left Antalya with no agreement?
Rather than a decision to build on the transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) roadmap initiated by Brazil, the only reference to fossil fuels remaining in the final text offered by Turkey was the industry’s favoured get-out-of jail-free technology – carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS).
The Australian government has already thrown its weight behind CCS, including special legislation to allow for offshore CO2 disposal, with virtually no evidence of its effectiveness. It is an open secret that the world’s biggest CCS project at Chevron’s Gorgon project has spectacularly failed to deliver but this has not stopped the government backing this failed technology.
We couldn’t even see the call for 35% electrification by 2035 be “clean” even with science clearly showing that if it’s not clean it will increase fossil gas use – adding a tenth of a degree of warming by mid-century.
Indeed, while the prime minister says every tenth of a degree of warming matters, his problem is that lowering every tenth of a degree of warming means his beloved gas industry loses more market share.
This week the WA premier, Roger Cook, jets off to Japan with gas giant Woodside – to talk up LNG markets.
It’s unlikely he’s going there to tell the LNG industry what’s needed to limit warming to 1.5C.
It’s also unlikely he’ll mention the International Energy Agency’s report last week showing that to limit warming to 1.5C, fossil gas demand falls by about 40% from 2025 levels by 2035, driven by rapid electrification of end-uses, efficiency improvements, and the displacement of gas-fired power generation by renewables.
Australians are looking to their federal and state governments to protect them from the terrifying ravages of climate change, yet those governments’ actions appear hyper-focused on fuelling more of it. And co-hosting the climate talks clearly didn’t help.
The government says it’s serious about climate action. By their fruits ye shall know them.
- Bill Hare, a physicist and climate scientist, is the chief executive of Climate Analytics

title: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’, experts find
article_text:
Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support systems that the population depends on for survival, according to a report.
Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination across the entire strip, the report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs) finds, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come.
Oxfam International’s executive director, Amitabh Behar, said: “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come.”
He said the “destruction and contamination of Gaza” have “fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival” and breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.
“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins … through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris. These risks will persist for generations to come, unless clean-up, remediation and recovery actions are prioritised.”
In 2025 and earlier this year, the UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. The Israeli mission in Geneva said Israel rejected the commission’s “libellous sham”. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.
Oxfam’s report gives the most comprehensive picture to date of what it calls the “toxic wasteland” created by the Israeli assault which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded at least 175,000, while thousands still remain unaccounted for under the rubble.
Using satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, it concludes contamination in Gaza is “widespread, severe and consequential, with serious implications for public health and civilian survival”.
Behar said: “It is horrifying to begin to understand the extent of toxic contamination being faced by the population, who can neither escape nor protect themselves properly from the dangers. In an area as small, oppressed and densely populated as Gaza, continuous exposure is inevitable, with people surrounded by waste and sewage, spreading pests and the risk of disease growing.
“Raw sewage is pouring into the sea and leaking into the ground, while the destruction of Gaza’s sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from the contamination around them.”
He added the “associated health consequences will be severe, with children and pregnant women among those facing the highest risks”.
The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates that Israel’s military operations have generated more than 61m tonnes of debris across the territory, turning Gaza’s destroyed homes, neighbourhoods and infrastructure into a vast reservoir of potentially hazardous materials.
The report’s author, Lama Abdul Samad, a global water and sanitation specialist at Oxfam, said tackling the environmental damage in Gaza will be “highly challenging because contamination is dispersed across the urban rubble, farmland, water systems and soils, while unexploded ordnance continues to restrict safe access to most areas”.
“The analysis highlights the urgent need for Israel to grant access for a detailed environmental assessment on the ground to clarify the risks to public health and identify options for urgent harm-reduction measures. Restoration is likely to require extensive clearance, monitoring and specialised remediation of affected areas from contaminants such as explosive residues, organic pollutants and heavy metals.”
Behar said that as international attention increasingly turned to Gaza’s reconstruction, environmental recovery must not be treated as an afterthought, but as a vital undertaking in parallel.
“Rebuilding Gaza without simultaneously understanding and addressing the extent of environmental contamination risks creating long-term public health consequences for generations to come,” he said.
A spokesperson from the Israeli embassy in the UK questioned the methodology underpinning the report, saying its reliance on satellite imagery and what they described as unverified assumptions “falls short of professional standards”.
They added: “Hamas itself claimed to have excavated more than 500 km of tunnels beneath Gaza, exceeding the total route length of the London Underground. A report on Gaza’s soil and groundwater that fails to examine excavation on that scale is fundamentally incomplete. That omission undermines the credibility of its conclusions.”

title: ‘Once installed, there’s no getting rid of it’: what Falklands oil plans mean for its seals, whales and penguins
article_text:
From the air, the main Falkland Islands form two large, jagged shapes against the South Atlantic. East Falkland and West Falkland are surrounded by 778 smaller islands and islets east of Patagonia’s southern tip.
The archipelago, a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina, is home to large colonies of albatrosses and penguins. Its waters, with those of the Patagonian shelf, provide feeding grounds for sea lions, southern elephant seals and southern right whales.
“We are talking about an area of great importance for wildlife, not only regionally but globally,” says Hernán Pérez Orsi, an oceans researcher, activist and energy coordinator at the Forum for the Conservation of the Patagonian Sea.
Yet new oil development plans licensed by the Falkland Islands government now threaten these waters: about 130 miles (210km) north of the islands lies the Sea Lion project, a major deepwater oil development that is likely to involve drilling wells and installing subsea infrastructure in the ocean.
Operated by Navitas Petroleum, with Rockhopper Exploration, the project plans 23 wells in its first two phases. Oil will be processed and stored onboard the Aoka Mizu, a production vessel with a planned capacity of up to 55,000 barrels a day.
The scale of Sea Lion and its potential effects on the environment concern the Argentine Association of Environmental Lawyers (AAdeAA). Noting that routine operations can cause marine pollution, Gonzalo Vergez, the organisation’s legal coordinator, says: “It is generally said that offshore oil operations cause harm, even when nothing goes wrong.”
Warnings have also come from the islands’ residents. In August 2024, Falklands Conservation, a local environmental organisation, questioned some of Sea Lion’s scientific data, used in its environmental impact statement.
Its report notes that birds from colonies hundreds or thousands of miles away, including albatrosses from South Georgia and New Zealand, visit Falklands’ waters, and says the only broadly appropriate seabird data in the impact statement is more than 20 years old. According to Falklands Conservation, good practice in regions such as the North Sea would require data collected within the past five years.
Oil exploration off the Falkland Islands is a new frontier in the South Atlantic rush driven by countries across Latin America and the Caribbean since Brazil discovered its largest oil reserves yet in deep waters up to 300 miles offshore in the 2000s.
While the British government has not provided direct financial support for the Sea Lion project, it offers political, diplomatic and legal backing. London maintains that Falklands residents have the right to self-determination, including the authority to manage their natural resources.
Recently, Ellie Reeves, the attorney general for England and Wales, said the Falkland Islands would suffer “devastating consequences” if the territory was blocked from developing the offshore oilfield.
The Patagonian shelf, where the islands lie, is one of the world’s most productive marine ecosystems, sustained by the cold, nutrient-rich waters of the Falkland current. A 2019 study led by the researcher Alastair Baylis estimates that the archipelago supports about three-quarters of the world’s black-browed albatross population, half of the global slender-billed prion population and about a third of the world’s southern rockhopper and gentoo penguin populations.
The researchers analysed 1,891 foraging trips by 686 animals from nine seabird and marine mammal species. They identified areas where several species’ ranges overlapped, especially on the Patagonian shelf north of the Falkland Islands.
“Our findings highlight that the distribution of marine predators on the Patagonian shelf [is] not constrained by national jurisdictions,” the researchers concluded.
Beyond the risk of a major accident, Sea Lion’s potential environmental threats range from minor oil leaks to underwater noise, drilling waste, industrial lighting and vessel traffic.
An oil spill would pose another danger: crude oil can poison animals and coat the feathers and fur of seabirds and marine mammals, impairing their ability to regulate their body temperature. Falklands Conservation’s report also questions the assessment of spill risks and the capacity to respond to an accident.
The project’s progress has also prompted a response from the Argentinian government, not for environmental reasons but against the backdrop of the long-running sovereignty dispute with the UK. On 3 September, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, signed a decree tightening controls on oil activities in the Falkland Islands without Argentinian authorisation.
Although his government promotes large-scale energy investment, the decree requires applicant companies and their affiliates to declare compliance with Argentinian legislation governing oil and gas activities in the islands.
The next day, the Argentinian presidency announced sanctions against 45 individuals and entities allegedly linked to those activities, including companies associated with Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, according to the Argentinian newspaper La Nación.
Environmental organisations, however, had been monitoring oil activity in these waters long before the government’s response. AAdeAA, headed by Enrique Viale, began investigating oil development in the Argentine Sea in 2020 and had been examining information about Sea Lion since at least 2024.
As the project advanced, it intensified its work and, on 1 September, joined the La Plata Falkland Islands Ex-Combatants Centre (CECIM), an organisation of Argentinian veterans of the 1982 war, in filing a preventive legal action over potential environmental damage in an attempt to halt the development.
“Once this project is installed, there is no getting rid of it,” Viale says.
The dispute also reached the Argentinian courts. On 16 September, the federal judge Mariel Borruto ordered Navitas and Rockhopper not to carry out any work until an environmental assessment had been conducted before the Argentinian authorities, or until the court ruled otherwise.
The injunction remained in force as of 29 October, although its enforcement is uncertain: the islands remain under British administration, beyond Argentina’s effective control.
Beyond the sovereignty dispute and the court rulings, questions remain about the project’s environmental impacts. Rockhopper declined to comment, directing inquiries to the project operator, Navitas.
Navitas stated that it would not comment on the allegations until the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea had ruled on a case brought by the Argentinian government against the UK, which claims that the Sea Lion project breaches Argentinian sovereignty and should be suspended. The court may hand down a decision on 28 November.
In its revised environmental impact statement from July 2025, Navitas acknowledged that some seabird survey data used was 24 years old, but argued it remained useful for identifying broad distribution patterns and had been supplemented by more recent research.
Although it acknowledged remaining data gaps, the company considers it impracticable for an operator to repeat surveys at this scale and has proposed collecting further data as the project develops.
The company also acknowledged potential impacts on marine wildlife even during routine operations. Its assessment rates the residual impacts and risks associated with artificial lighting, underwater noise, the discharge of drill cuttings and vessel collisions with cetaceans as “moderate”, despite the proposed mitigation measures.
Navitas has proposed vessel speed restrictions and the use of specialist seabird and marine mammal observers, while acknowledging that visual monitoring cannot prevent collisions in darkness. It rates its confidence in the collision risk assessment as “uncertain”.
In the event of an oil spill, the document also acknowledges the challenges of responding in the south Atlantic’s difficult sea conditions: in one modelled scenario of a subsea well blowout, recovery equipment was projected to recover just 6.3% of the spilt oil, without reducing the estimated amount reaching the shoreline.
As the Sea Lion project moves towards oil production, environmental organisations warn about the consequences for one of the richest marine ecosystems in the south Atlantic.
For Vergez, the uncertainty provides all the more reason to act. “In the absence of scientific certainty,” he says, “the principles of prevention and precaution apply: protection is necessary.”

title: Country diary: Top deck of the bus for the finest views of autumn | John Gilbey
article_text:
The morning starts bright but cold, with a hazy mist clinging to the trees across the valley. This could be one of the last good weather days, so I take the bus north into Gwynedd, clambering awkwardly upstairs to get the best view of the autumn colours.
The mist begins to clear and, in a wet meadow, a heron stands alertly by a ditch, watching for movement. Beyond the Afon Dyfi, the hills are golden with patches of larch and the deeper orange tones of the oak and ash. Well-defined shadows below the dark blue sky shelter pockets of still-frosted gloom, as we cross the Dyfi into Gwynedd.
Traversing the col beyond the village of Corris, the land drops away to reveal the great buttressed rampart of Cadair Idris. Ochre swathes of bracken coat the slopes, cut by stone walls then edged with tongues of scree and stunted trees. Passing clouds block and channel the light, prising apart the almost hidden ridges like the tabs in a child’s model theatre.
Winter pasture patched with rush and gorse dominates the descent towards Cross Foxes, while the easterly view of the Cadair range reinforces its steep northern scarps. A quick pause in Dolgellau’s Eldon Square – no time to grab a pasty, sadly – and we’re off again, crossing the Afon Mawddach and climbing through wooded valleys into the high, undulating plateau of the Harlech Dome.
To the west, beyond scrub-mottled rough grazing, a jagged line of ancient Cambrian geology hangs over the landscape – the peaks of Rhinog Fach and Rhinog Fawr, painfully familiar from my youthful scrambles. The long, straight road that rolls down towards Trawsfynydd presages the incongruous, slightly sinister appearance of two brutalist monoliths – once a nuclear power plant – squatting troll-like by the lake.
Decanted from the bus on the outskirts of Porthmadog, I take a moment to look around. High cloud is beginning to cover the western sky, and a bitter wind slices across the estuary of the Afon Glaslyn. A skein of geese creaks eastward overhead, and I begin to edge my way round the tree-bound knoll to begin my walk. But that, as they say, is another story.

title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
article_text:
In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend.
Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Despite their reservations, others – notably China and the African group – were prepared to accept a flawed package to keep multilateralism alive.
While the failure to agree Cop31’s “cover decision” dominated the summit’s headlines, other decisions did pass. The work on a just transition will continue for three years, but the mechanism to make it operational is missing. There was progress on how to assess adaptation needs for developing nations, but not on how to pay for it. Such gaps highlight the unresolved political conflicts at the heart of the UN talks.
An agreement to transition away from fossil fuels was made in 2023. A tripling of adaptation finance was promised in 2025. Yet the Australian-Turkish joint presidency diverted attention away from delivering these commitments towards a cover decision promoting controversial technologies and electrification without tying this to renewable energy. The latter has an energy-security rationale: disruption from the US-Israel war on Iran strengthens the case for replacing imported fossil fuels with homegrown electricity. But how that electricity is generated matters – and poorer countries need support to fund the switch.
Wealthy nations don’t have much of a moral pedestal upon which to lecture them. The UK government is spending less on climate finance per year over the next three years than it did over the last five and is expected to give a nod to Rosebank – the biggest undeveloped oilfield in UK waters – by the end of 2026. More egregiously, Sweden’s environment minister, Romina Pourmokhtari, who led the EU’s finance group at Cop31, publicly backed a weakening of the country’s emissions rules that lay behind its 7% greenhouse gas increase in 2024.
The UN process remains the only forum where every country has a voice and an opportunity to shape outcomes. Before the next Cop, in Ethiopia, trust between parties must be repaired through a transparent negotiating process. Strenuous efforts must also be made to avoid last-minute wrangling over a text that displaces the original agreed agenda by making progress on turning finance pledges into action.
This year brought glacier collapses, record European heat and wildfires across Asia. The world must do much more to confront a human-made catastrophe. It is unarguable that fossil fuels are the primary cause of global heating. What is required is a fair and equitable transition on a global scale to cleaner energy. “The climate crisis will not wait for governments to find common ground. Neither can we,” said UN secretary general António Guterres. It is impossible to disagree.

title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
article_text:
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.
The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.
Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”
Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.
“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.
The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.
Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.
“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”
Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.
The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”
Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.
The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.
A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

title: ‘When it roars, we roar back’: the man who faces Bengal tigers armed only with a stick
article_text:
At the age of 15, Abdul Goni Gazi had an experience that would alter the course of his life. It began as a fishing trip with his brother, deep within the Sundarbans, a vast landscape of mangrove forest, rivers and islands stretching across the tidal delta of Bangladesh and India.
“We went to the riverbank to cut firewood for cooking,” he says. “I was standing there holding the boat in place, while looking towards the bank.”
Relaxed and happy, he closed his eyes for a moment. But when he opened them, the feeling of tranquility evaporated. “Suddenly, a tiger appeared in front of me.”
A fully grown Bengal tiger had been stalking the brothers, waiting for the perfect moment to strike.
“I quickly loosened the boat and moved out toward the middle of the river. My elder brother saw the tiger, dived into the river, swam toward the middle, and climbed into the boat. By then, I had fainted from fear.”
Nowadays Gazi, 45, is known locally as “Goni Tiger” and is a prominent advocate for tiger and human coexistence. His early terror turned to fascination.
“I heard stories from my father about protecting people from tigers,” he says. “From those stories, a passion for protecting tigers grew in me.”
At first his focus was on the humans they attacked. In about 2007, a tiger killed two people from the town of Satkhira in Bangladesh, and Gazi accompanied the conservation organisation Forest Tiger Response Team to recover the bodies. During the mission two workers were killed and another severely injured.
Nevertheless, Goni decided that he was interested in the work and, after providing unofficial support to a similar organisation called Wild Team, he was offered a role.
Gazi says that, as tiger attacks continued, his work became a balance between going out to recover people who had been attacked, and keeping the tigers alive.
By his reckoning he has helped save 36 tigers and recovered the bodies of 106 attack victims. Whether encouraging a tiger to return to the forest or to abandon a body, his methods are strikingly low-tech and non-lethal.
“If the tiger becomes aggressive in a neighbourhood, we pretend to be aggressive back,” he says. “When it roars, we roar back. Because the tiger thinks us scary now, it leaves the neighbourhood, or the individual. And so it survives.” On other occasions, he tranquillises the tiger and gets it back to the wild.
His reputation has grown over the years, but so has the pressure on tigers, bringing increased conflict with humans. Despite the uptick in danger and work, by 2019, funding for Wild Team had dried up. So, Gazi created a 21-person crew, mostly volunteers, that he trains himself. “And we rescue everything: tigers, snakes … everything.”
But the danger remains real, as Gazi illustrates by describing the recovery of a man called Nab Dada. Gazi and his team walked for miles through a largely dry canal, following blood and other signs left by the tiger. It was eerily silent, he recalls, save for the sporadic crack of twigs, and smaller animals scuffling away. They found the body but there was one issue: the tiger was still nearby. “Although we couldn’t see it, we could hear it,” he says.
As he lifted the body on to his shoulders, his friend Shahin said: “‘Goni, there is a tiger behind you.’ I turned around and saw the tiger,” Gazi recalls. “I became very frightened, but I shouted and looked directly into the tiger’s eyes. I used my stick to frighten it.” Not to be outdone, the tiger roared, but Gazi and his team stood their ground and the big cat gave up.
The team began the journey back carrying the body. “As we were walking back, the tiger came after us two or three times. Each time, we drove it away again and continued carrying the body.
“The force of a tiger’s roar and its appearance when you are standing there facing it is something extremely difficult. It is very, very difficult to describe in words.”
Tiger numbers in Bangladesh were estimated at 106 in 2015, 114 in 2018 and 125 in the 2024 census. Habitat loss, poaching and climate breakdown remain significant concerns. Rising sea levels, increasingly powerful storms and greater salinity are degrading land around the forest, while human development is pushing people further into tiger habitat, leading to more conflicts.
The loss of lives has made the ecological importance of tigers to the Sundarbans hard for some people to accept. Gazi believes his work has contributed to changing those attitudes.
“At one time, the people in my area wanted there to be no more tigers,” he says. “But I wanted the tigers to survive. When a tiger comes from the Sundarbans into our villages, the people in my community now also help send it back into the Sundarbans instead of killing it.”
That shift has not come without resistance. “In trying to save tigers, I have been insulted many times and I have even been beaten,” he says. “Even so, my goal is to save them. This is work that I have to do for my country. Wildlife belongs to every one of us.
“If the tiger survives, the Sundarbans survives,” he says. “If the Sundarbans survives, the people of the world survive.”
