title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
article_text:
On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought. Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.
Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.
The trials aim to identify robust apple varieties that are resistant to diseases and pests, crop reliably and can withstand the most extreme weather that might affect Somerset.
“Somerset is the best county in the world for making cider. But the climate is changing. It has been changing for a long time. We need to be in a position where we’ve got the experience, the knowledge and the trees in place to deal with those changes,” says Martin Thatcher, the company’s managing director.
One of the biggest challenges he faces is the length of time it takes to introduce a new apple variety and change growing methods in orchards. “It doesn’t happen overnight. Each apple tree takes seven years to get to a fruit crop and could last 40 years. So it takes a very long time [for experiments] to come to fruition,” he says.
The trials came about because, nearly 30 years ago, his father, John Thatcher, rescued 458 varieties of cider apples grown at the Long Ashton research station, a government-funded horticultural and agricultural research centre founded in 1903. “My father took cuttings of every single variety before the centre was closed down, so we have an orchard with 458 varieties in it.”
The collection includes traditional cider apples and newer varieties that cater for modern tastes. “We’re looking at that orchard now and first of all seeing which apples make fabulous cider. And then we’re looking at how the trees are doing under modern orchard conditions – and if they’re good healthy trees and they’re cropping, we will plant them out in rows of 100-tree trials, to future-proof our orchard growing.”
He is trying to use fewer pesticides, so is keen to find varieties that are naturally resistant to disease and pests, and will blossom at exactly the moment when spring conditions suit apple tree pollinators such as bumblebees and honeybees.
Another priority is to find varieties that need less winter chill in a warming climate: apple trees, he explains, need a sustained cold period in winter to complete their dormancy, which enables their fruit buds to develop properly in spring. “That winter chill is really important – and last year, we probably didn’t have quite enough, and some varieties are more susceptible to a lack of winter chill than others.”
Thatchers’ orchard manager, Chris Muntz Torres, says jonagold, a cross between golden delicious and a jonathan apple, performed particularly well in trials this year. “They’ve got this vigour, this willingness to grow, whatever the weather.”
He thinks this is because the tree’s vigorous growth above ground is matched by a strong root system. “That’s what we want – a variety that, irrespective of the weather, is robust enough to grow.”
Myrtle Farm has also begun planting wildflower strips in its orchards, to attract insects that prey on pests such as the rosy apple aphid – a strategy that research has shown could save apple growers up to £3,000 a hectare every year and support native pollinators.
Nigel Jenner, head of agronomy for tree fruit at the global fruit producer AM Fresh UK, works with independent apple farmers, who represent about 30% of Britain’s apple-growing industry. He says roughly 70% of these growers – about 220 – have planted wildflower strips in the past five years, and that number is increasing.
“We know this is the way forward,” Jenner says. “It works and it has a meaningful effect on your chemical input and your spray bill.”
He hopes seed producers will soon develop an “orchard mix” of wildflowers designed to attract the beneficial insects that apple growers need, and produce enough of it to bring prices down and make the practice even more widespread.
Many independent growers are also experimenting with new methods of water management, Jenner says. “Years ago, you’d kick the soil and say ‘oh that’s a bit dry, we’ll water it’. Now, we’re using neutron probes to measure the water deficit and we’re trying to get the trees to hunt for water.”
This involves letting the trees become water-stressed, he says: the top 65mm of soil in an orchard is left to dry out, which encourages deeper root growth and reduces the need for irrigation.
Back at Myrtle Farm, Thatchers is also working to improve soil health through regenerative farming. Before any trees are planted in new orchards, herbal leys – mixtures of grasses, legumes and deep-rooted herbs such as chicory – are sown and the land is grazed by sheep.
“Their little feet pound the ground, which improves the soil structure, and they eat the herbal ley and then recycle it very effectively back into the ground, which also improves the soil structure. So where we’ve had fields that have been continuous cereals or maize, we’ve found that within three years, the soil on all the metrics that are important for growing apples improves by at least 20%,” says Thatcher.
The 14,000 young trees planted in this regenerated soil in March 2025 are “doing absolutely fantastically through two very dry years” with a survival rate above 99.9%, says Muntz Torres. “We’re looking at a field which is full of diversity in the soil, so any moisture that we do get, the organic matter in the soil holds it there and keeps the soil more healthy. It acts like a sponge.”
The apple tree roots are following the strong, deep-burrowing chicory roots down into the soil, he adds. “There’s this whole biological exchange within the soil structure, which means that root growth isn’t impeded. The roots release sugars into the soil, that feeds the microbes and the microbes give nutrients back to the roots.”
Like Thatchers, Jenner’s growers have also been planting new apple cultivars in the hope of producing more disease-resistant and environmentally friendly apples, he says.
“One is called magic star, which is a fantastic apple. It’s a firm, juicy, red apple – and it’s resistant to scab, which is the main disease apple growers have to spray against every seven to 10 days.”
Although this year has been challenging, the changing climate has also brought new opportunities for his growers, he says, and some are now experimenting with varieties that typically grow in much warmer countries, such as Australia.
“We’re now growing Pink Lady apples over here very successfully. If you’d said you were going to grow Pink Lady 10 years ago, you would have been laughed at.”

title: Surgery by fairy lights and truckloads of fruit: the sanctuary saving Cameroon’s chimpanzees
article_text:
Every morning in central Cameroon, the primatologist Sheri Speede wakes to a daunting task. At the Sanaga-Yong sanctuary, which she founded in 1999, there are 75 chimpanzees to feed four times a day and monitor for physical or behavioural issues.
Of those, more than 30 need to be given routine birth-control medications, four are babies requiring round-the-clock care, and two are rowdy teenagers currently being integrated into new social groups.
A chimpanzee might wake up on the wrong side of the bed and decide to pick a fight, hatch a plan to rise in the group hierarchy, or refuse to take its medication. On any given day, Speede is therapist, meal-prepper, veterinarian and site manager all in one.
Originally a veterinarian in the US, Speede visited Cameroon in the late 1990s and, in 1997, met Jacky, a chimpanzee that had been kept in a small cage outside a hotel in Limbe for nearly 30 years. Known around town as the “mad chimpanzee”, Jacky had little prospect of release or rehabilitation. In August 1999, Speede brought Jacky to her newly founded sanctuary, where he became one of Sanaga-Yong’s first three residents.
Jacky is still there, estimated to be in his 60s. He and Speede have lived side-by-side for a quarter of a century – longer than many people live with their own children.
The problem, though, as it has been for decades, is that chimpanzees and other great apes are hunted as some of the most prized bushmeat species in the world. The practice is deeply rooted in traditional remedies, with a reported 36 conditions claimed to be healed by 22 chimpanzee parts. Female chimp reproductive organs are said to cure infertility in women; crushed bones, to heal fractures; sleeping on their skins, to offer protection during childbirth.
Poaching is often a two-for-one transaction. When mothers and mature adults are killed for meat, their infants are sold to wealthy clients who want a chimpanzee as a pet, or to the private zoo trade. Compounding this is the near-absence of government enforcement against wildlife trafficking.
In addition, the decades-long armed conflict in Cameroon has harmed biodiversity conservation in the country. Between the anglophone crisis – an ongoing armed conflict between the Cameroonian government in the south-west and separatist groups in the north-west – and the Boko Haram insurgency, many of the country’s conservationists and forests are being badly affected. Every time the government launches a counterattack on separatist groups in the north-west, civilian villages are burned and hundreds of people flee the violence, seeking shelter in the forests – forests that were once the natural habitat of endangered great apes.
Armed groups also often take up temporary residence in the shelter and secrecy of Cameroon’s dense forests. There, they set traps for bushmeat and carve out farms in previously protected areas. As armed groups regularly control the movement of people and goods in the area, regardless of what side of the conflict they are on, their presence greatly restricts the ability of conservationists to continue their work.
Cameroon is home to the Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee, of which conservation groups estimate somewhere between 3,500 and 9,000 remain in the wild. Classified as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, and one of humanity’s closest living relatives, the subspecies continues to decline as the bushmeat trade goes largely unpoliced by the Cameroonian government. Killing chimpanzees has been illegal in the country since 1994, but enforcement effectively began only in 2006, pushed by the Last Great Ape organisation (Laga). The NGO says it has recorded more than a hundred great ape confiscations – dead and alive – annually since then. An estimated five to 10 chimpanzees are lost for every one recovered.
That gap between law and enforcement has not closed. Paul Biya has led Cameroon’s government since 1982, making him one of the longest-serving non-royal heads of state, and under his administration the burden of humanitarian and conservation work has fallen largely to international organisations rather than the state.
Cameroon’s safeguarded chimpanzee population is mostly at three wildlife centres – Ape Action Africa, Sanaga-Yong Chimpanzee Rescue and Limbe Wildlife Centre. Together they house well over 200 rescued chimpanzees, with no plan or space to release them, for lack of enforcement to safeguard them and appropriate forested habitat. For this reason female chimpanzees at Sanaga-Yong are given birth control medication.
As the fight continues for chimpanzee conservation and stricter anti-poaching laws in Cameroon, Sanaga-Yong stands as a stronghold. The sanctuary has earned wide recognition for some of the best chimpanzee care in the world. It runs on a model that benefits the surrounding community, with all of its caregivers hired locally. In recent years it has taken on two Cameroonian veterinarians, Mael Firina and Christian Atonfack, who joined the team upon graduation from veterinary school. While many sanctuaries rotate through international staff, the goal here is to train both vets under Speede and visiting international veterinarians so that the sanctuary’s future veterinary care rests in Cameroonian hands.
That localisation of talent is increasingly the model for conservation. When the work of protecting a place is put in the hands of the people who live there, the odds of it lasting go up considerably.
“Conservation led by Indigenous peoples and local communities, based on their own knowledge and tenure systems, is far more likely to deliver positive outcomes for nature,” says Neil Dawson, a global development researcher at the University of East Anglia who has studied the role of Indigenous people and local communities in conservation. “In fact, conservation very often fails because it excludes and undervalues local knowledge and this often infringes on rights and cultural diversity along the way.”

title: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?
article_text:
Stand on the coastline at high tide and you look out over unbroken water, with sandy islands rising a few miles offshore. A few hours later and the view across the Wadden Sea has transformed into a maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes and mud flats.
As the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world, this ever-changing habitat stretches hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands and was awarded world heritage status by Unesco in 2009.
But, 17 years later, the Wadden Sea is a step closer to finding itself on Unesco’s world heritage in danger list. As a result of “continuing uncertainty surrounding the cumulative impacts of multiple pressures affecting the property … as well as indications of increasing ecosystem stress and ecological degradation”, the UN body is expected to send a joint inspection mission with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) to the Wadden Sea in 2027 to assess the state of its conservation.
Squeezed behind a string of islands, from Fanø in Denmark to Texel in the Netherlands, the Wadden Sea is a vital staging post on the migratory route of millions of birds, and hosts thousands of species of marine creatures and plants.
It is also, across the three countries, home to hundreds of thousands of people on many islands, as well as towns and villages on the mainland.
But, according to experts, human activities, from salt and gas extraction to fishing, tourism and even military exercises (there is a Nato bombing range on the Dutch island of Vlieland) are putting pressure on the Wadden Sea.
For Wouter van der Heij, a marine biologist who works for the Dutch environmental organisation Waddenvereniging, it adds up to “a very vulnerable situation”.
“The numbers of birds are going down, the amount of fish is going down, the biodiversity on the mudflats, it’s going down,” he says.
If the Wadden Sea joins the danger list, it would be among just a handful of European sites, which would be a huge embarrassment for the authorities and a serious blow to the many residents, particularly on the islands, who make their living from tourism.
Aant van der Veen has lived on Vlieland, which has a population of just over 1,000 people, his whole life. One of his businesses takes tours around the island.
“If we lose the tourism on the islands, then it doesn’t matter what you’re doing, everybody’s going bankrupt,” he says.
Van der Veen is sitting outside parliament in The Hague, as part of a group representing residents across the Dutch Wadden Sea that has been meeting members of the House of Representatives, the lower house of the Dutch parliament.
Earlier this year, maps were circulated, apparently showing that large parts of the Wadden could be closed off to islanders and visitors in order to reach conservation targets.
A post from Van der Veen on Facebook sparked a “We are the Wadden” campaign, with flags and banners adorning villages across the islands at the height of holiday season. It generated lots of media attention and a petition signed by more than 50,000 people – hence the parliamentary meeting.
“Six months ago, we did not have a voice,” he says. “Now we have the voice of almost 52,000 people.”
The Dutch authorities have acknowledged a failure of communication and promised to involve local people more fully in future decisions.
“People have lived and worked in and alongside the natural environment of the Wadden Sea for centuries,” a Dutch government spokesperson said. “The starting point is that this will remain possible in the future and that this balance will not be fundamentally altered.”
But, they added: “The area must remain livable for future generations, and multifunctional use must continue to be possible.
“World heritage status was granted in 2009, encompassing all activities that were already taking place at that time. We will continue to advocate this fact to Unesco.”
The Dutch aren’t the only people with responsibility for the Wadden Sea. Management is the joint responsibility of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark. But there are many layers of regulation and protection, at local, regional, national and European level, and huge differences in how, and by whom, they are enforced.
Mona Friedrich is a campaigner with the Environmental Justice Foundation, which is taking legal action in part of the German Wadden Sea to try to enforce European regulations on assessing the environmental impact of bottom trawling.
“[The Wadden Sea] has multiple layers of protection on paper – it’s a national park, a Unesco world heritage site and it’s part of the Natura 2000 network – and still bottom trawling continues to be authorised,” she says.
“It is very complicated to find out who’s responsible for what agency, what’s done at federal level, what’s done at state level. It always takes a long time to figure out who is responsible for what.”
Van der Heij says one of the greatest threats to the ecology of the Wadden Sea is that rising sea levels and subsidence from extraction could lead to the mudflats remaining covered, even at low tide.
“If they are no longer dry during low tides and no longer available for migratory birds to find their food, [then their] route, the East Atlantic Flyway, will be in danger because the birds are no longer able to migrate all the way,” he says.
Van der Heij adds that taking gas and salt from under the Wadden Sea can lead to subsidence, potentially threatening the drying banks, which is why the Waddenvereniging recently coordinated an “Urgent call for help” to Unesco.
It asked the UN body to “take a strong stand” against draft approval for proposals to extend salt extraction under the sea near Harlingen. A final decision is expected shortly from the Dutch authorities, who point to the “hand-on-tap” method of monitoring subsidence – in other words, if it goes beyond set limits, work must be stopped.
The government recently refused permission for gas to be taken from the Ternaard field, which lies between the Dutch coast and the island of Ameland, despite pressures on European energy supplies, a decision welcomed by Unesco and campaigners.
But renewable energy projects also pose a threat to the mudflats, say campaigners. The huge windfarms being built offshore in the North Sea need to be connected to the grid, and that means laying cables across the mudflats and under (or through) islands such as Schiermonnikoog in the Netherlands or Baltrum and Langeoog in Germany.
Despite protections built into the system, which limit where and when work can take place, it is another pressure on the Wadden Sea, says Van der Heij.
“If you introduce these activities, but are stopping others, then it would be a transition, but at this moment it’s just adding [to] what’s already happening,” he says.
“So they are still mining for gas and salt. They are still fishing. They are still dredging the gullies for shipping lanes. So you end up with, again, a new activity with harmful effects on nature.”
It is that cumulative effect that concerns Van der Veen and his fellow islanders – and the possibility that their needs might be sacrificed.
“I think one of the biggest concerns is that they will allow all those big things to happen and then say, ‘Oh, but we can compensate [by] restricting the area for the people that live there, or the tourists,’” he says.
“We don’t want to be the change in that bargain.”

title: First guidelines on attempts to manipulate the ocean put spotlight on geoengineering industry
article_text:
A cluster of candy cane-striped smoke stacks dots the horizon of Tufts Cove in Nova Scotia, Canada. Deep in the briny depths of Halifax harbour, something huge is happening: the ocean is being engineered to remove atmospheric carbon.
“This is what Mother Nature has done naturally for a few billion years in order to rebalance the atmospheric and ocean chemistry over long timescales,” says Dr Greg Rau, co-founder and senior scientist at Planetary Technologies.
Planetary Technologies is an ocean carbon-removal firm and one of a growing number of companies attempting to decrease excess atmospheric carbon – the main driver of the climate crisis – by speeding up naturally occurring carbon cycles in the ocean.
To do this, the company conducts ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE), adding a chalk-like substance to the seawater, which allows the water to absorb and store more atmospheric carbon than usual.
This process also helps to offset ocean acidification, often called the “evil twin” of the climate crisis, which is increasing dramatically.
Because it relies on an already occurring process, proponents say these technologies will not harm the marine creatures that call this harbour home, such as mackerel, sunfish, harbour seals and sea turtles. But some marine scientists worry that adding any extra materials to an already stressed ecosystem might harm aquatic life and say that this field of marine geoengineering needs more research.
“If we develop a new medicine, you have steps that you’re supposed to take. You don’t just find a substance and just implement it,” says Sam Dupont, a senior lecturer at the University of Gothenburg. “And at the moment, with [ocean carbon removal] it seems you’re jumping to clinical trial immediately.”
Planetary Technologies runs its operations five days a week. Working out of a shipping container, it adds an alkaline slurry, its proprietary formula, to a local power company’s cooling water to create an odourless milky composite, which is then discharged into Halifax harbour and monitored by their sensors.
Bolstered initially by small government grants, venture funds and other private capital, Planetary Technologies now generates revenue by selling carbon-removal credits worth millions of dollars to companies such as JPMorgan Chase and Shopify.
Ocean carbon removal is a fledgling industry but one that has seen more than $500m (£370m) invested since 2021, according to Ocean Carbon Removal Watch, a database launched by the Pulitzer Center, which tracks marine carbon dioxide removal (mCDR) investments.
After over a decade of protracted negotiations among scores of countries, this October the International Maritime Organization (IMO) adopted the first international framework that officially acknowledges the three major ocean carbon removal techniques: ocean fertilisation, ocean alkalinity enhancement and biomass sinking.
Adopted in London during the annual meeting of the London convention and protocol, a little-known but influential treaty that governs the dumping of waste at sea, the new framework urged a cautionary approach. The IMO said in a statement that “further scientific research is needed before any activities beyond the research stage can be considered”. But it acknowledged that “marine geoengineering is attracting increasing scientific, commercial and public attention”.
“The IMO assessments are sending a strong signal to governments and industry alike that this is something that we, as a global community, prioritise,” says Fatima Candace Vahlsing, vice-president for climate at Ocean Conservancy, a US-based nonprofit organisation. “Whether you’re a business or an academic or a nonprofit, everyone wants the system to work and there to be trust around the system.”
However, some scientists and conservation organisations fear the private-sector market is moving ahead too fast and risks creating technologies that damage the ocean and potentially cloud the sector before real breakthroughs are made.
Brad Ack, chief executive of Ocean Visions, a conservation organisation that promotes creative solutions to conserve and restore the ocean, says the sector needs significant public investment to set rules and standards.
“That’s largely being done by the private sector and the academic sector at this point, and that’s not enough,” he says. Government funding, particularly in the United States, where this sector began, has increasingly dried up.
Nova Scotia, known for its cod fishing history and legendary tides, is now the largest ocean alkalinity-enhancement centre in the world. Anchored by Dalhousie University’s Ocean Frontier Institute and bolstered by grants from the Canadian government and partnerships with research institutions in Germany and Australia, the private companies CarbonRun and pHathom Technologies are also operating there, in addition to a test site run by Carbon to Sea, a non-profit scientific research programme.
But as the Halifax hub continues to grow, and other field trials are proposed across the world in places as varied as the Gulf of Mexico, the Gulf off Saudi Arabia, Norway’s rivers or the harbours of Singapore, the wider field continues to face questions. Since the sector is so new, it is unclear how existing maritime laws can be applied, for example, and where exactly their jurisdiction starts.
“This creates opportunities for bad actors to exploit gaps in the regulatory regimes,” says Romany Webb, deputy director of the New York-based Sabin Center for Climate Change Law.
At the same time that governance is being negotiated, scientists are realising that the base materials used for alkalinity enhancement are not created equally. Some materials, such as byproducts from mining, are considerably cheaper but the trace metals in them can have an outsized impact on marine ecosystems.
“Even in very low concentrations, you can have toxic effects with trace metals,” says Nina Bednaršek, a senior scientist at Slovenia’s Jožef Stefan Institute, which specialises in biological risk assessment for mCDR. Bednaršek worries especially about zooplankton, which are the base of the marine food chain.
Although there are scientists investigating the environmental impacts of alkalinity enhancement on marine life, it remains understudied globally.
Bednaršek is working with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) to develop a methodology for accounting for carbon removal through ocean alkalinity enhancement which, similar to the recently released IMO framework, which would help with environmental safeguards and regulatory oversight.
“Right now, there is no price on the biology,” says Bednaršek. “I think that’s wrong.”
Lisa Levin, professor emeritus at California’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography, agrees. “For ocean alkalinity enhancement, most of the research has examined consequences for ocean chemistry, which I don’t consider an assessment of environmental risk,” she says.
But many of those involved in the business of carbon removal argue more legislation means more delay in scaling up the industry, which is time the ocean, and the planet, do not have.
“Conservation tends to sort of have this kneejerk reaction that any time you do anything in the ocean … out of the ordinary, it’s got to be bad,” says Rau at Planetary Technologies.
“They need to understand that we’re beyond that point here – we are damaging the ocean. You can put all the fences you want around a certain area of the ocean, but it’s going to warm and it’s going to acidify.”
Additional reporting by Allison Gacad. This story was produced in partnership with the Pulitzer Center and with the support of an Alicia Patterson fellowship

title: This small Alaska town is swamped by cruise ship visitors every summer. But what happens when they all go home?
article_text:
October comes to the small Alaska coastal town of Skagway like a sigh. The shops that were bustling throughout the crazed tourist season are reducing their opening hours or beginning to close. The hordes of employees sleeping in overcrowded bunkhouses are leaving or have left.
The crowds of cruise passengers who have filled the streets since April, wearing lanyards emblazoned with the names of their ships, have dwindled to a trickle. Soon, they will all be gone. Snow is visible on the nearby mountains.
What is left after the season has ended and the last ship has disappeared from sight is a year-round community of about 1,100 people – on paper, at least – and the concern that, as the demands of the cruise ship industry grow, life in this small town is becoming more and more difficult.
“The year-round economy, the year-round population is one of my bigger concerns as someone who lives here,” says Skagway’s mayor, Orion Hanson. “What does Skagway do without a coffee shop to congregate in or without a restaurant open all the time? We don’t have a diner any more.”
Two local restaurants stay open, albeit with limited hours outside the cruise ship season. But the Sweet Tooth cafe, once a longstanding year-round diner, is gone. It is now a storefront for Diamonds International, a tax-free jewellery store that partners with cruise lines for onboard retail and shops in ports that open seasonally.
At the height of the Klondike gold rush, Skagway was the largest town in Alaska, with a population of about 10,000 people. In 1900, it became Alaska’s first official city. But by 1910, as the gold rush subsided, the population had dwindled to about 600 people.
It took a decade for that dramatic swing. Now, as one of the most popular cruise ship destinations in the world, it can happen in a single day, when thousands can flood on to Skagway’s streets from cruise ships, only to leave again when the sun sets. The most recent figures available show that more than 1.35 million tourists arrived in Skagway by cruise ship in 2025, alongside more than half a million crew – and the numbers are growing each year.
That means housing, services and infrastructure designed for a town of about 1,000 people having to accommodate an influx of thousands of workers who arrive in late winter and stay until early autumn.
“Part of the complication of Skagway is that you have such a boom in the summer and such a lull in the winter,” says Hanson. “In terms of revenue that’s not directly related to cruise ships there is not a lot.
“As we saw during the pandemic, we’re at risk,” he says. “If all your eggs are in one basket, it leaves you very vulnerable.”
Like many tourist towns, Skagway has a housing shortage. Unlike other towns, however, it is squeezed into a narrow valley set at the northern end of Alaska’s Inside Passage, a 500-mile maritime route that hugs the coast along Alaska and British Columbia. It is known for its rugged mountains, forests, glaciers and abundant wildlife; there are no realistic commuting options and no room to expand – the only road leads to Canada.
The Skagway Development Corporation commissioned a report in 2023 that found there were 644 housing units in town. In the years since, more have been added, but not enough for the town to accommodate the cruise ship industry and the businesses that support it, its permanent residents, seasonal employees and the workers and families who keep Skagway’s essential services running.
As a result, everything from warehouses to single-family homes, from tents to recreational vehicles or motorhomes, are accommodating the increasing numbers of seasonal workers each year.
“There’s a lot of congregate living and couch surfing,” says Al Wall, director of the town’s Dahl Memorial Clinic. “There are quite a few people that sleep in hammocks in the woods. And frankly, some would prefer to sleep in a hammock in a tree than stay in a crowded place with a bunch of people.”
In years past, many seasonal workers slept in camp sites. But a change in the town’s law forbidding season-long camping pushed them into traditional homes that previously housed the town’s established population.
Janilyn Heger, a longtime Skagwegian, owns the town’s distillery, Skagway Spirits. She and her husband Gary, who owns a construction company, once managed the town-owned camp sites.
“The city made the decision for whatever reason to abandon that type of housing, and that created a domino effect that has been a disaster for the community,” she says.
“Employers started buying buildings and displacing year-round housing and so now we’re at an absolute standstill. There’s none to be had.”
Skagway’s housing shortage has become so severe that many of the town’s limited hotels have been converted into accommodation for seasonal employees.
Longtime resident Mike Healy bought Sergeant Preston’s hotel from friends when he was unable to find land to build enough employee housing to meet his businesses’ needs.
“I didn’t want to purchase Sergeant Preston’s … I approached the city and said, hey, Municipality of Skagway, I am going to purchase the only year-round hotel in this community if you don’t free up some land for housing.” At the time Healy purchased Sergeant Preston’s, the town also had a year-round bed and breakfast.
Healy, not receiving an answer, duly converted the hotel into seasonal housing, part of a portfolio that provides off-season accommodation to visiting workers and contractors.
Jonathan Hillis, a town assembly member who owns the local Mountain Shop outdoor gear store, says that pattern is playing out across town.
“We have very few places now for independent travellers to stay, which is fostering this kind of cycle of more and more cruise ship tourists and fewer independent travellers.”
The scale of cruise tourism is a frequent topic of debate in towns throughout the Inside Passage. As the 2026 season winds down, these towns are consulting the docking schedules for 2027 and 2028, making note of the projected increase in tourism, and asking how much they can realistically handle.
One hundred miles south of Skagway in Alaska’s capital, Juneau, there have been repeated attempts to limit cruise ship tourism. After a ballot measure for “ship-free Saturdays” failed in 2024, the city introduced a voluntary limit on the number of ships that could dock daily.
Farther south in the Inside Passage, Ketchikan has reported more ships as a result of cruises adhering to Juneau’s limitations, while Sitka, also on the cruise ship destination trail, is reviewing its agreements with the industry after an anticipated increase in visitor numbers in 2027.
A survey conducted by Oregon State University reveals a nuanced position when it comes to the cruise sector in Skagway. Just over 40% of people who responded thought that the benefits of tourism outweighed the costs, compared with 25% who put it the other way round. Another 33% viewed the relationship as roughly balanced.
Whatever the sentiment, for a small town that is economically dependent on one industry for its livelihood, options are limited.
“There’s only so much we can do, even if we wanted to,” Hanson says. “We need to be incredibly careful about not rocking the boat.”

title: ‘No one cares about the little guy’: plastic nurdles still washing ashore in Sri Lanka five years after toxic spill
article_text:
On the beach in Pamunugama, on Sri Lanka’s west coast, women in uniform work under the scorching sun. They sift through rubbish washed ashore, searching among the usual litter for something much smaller: tiny plastic pellets.
Five years ago, in May 2021, this same beach was swamped with pellets as smoke rose over the Indian Ocean.
In May 2021, after the MV X-Press Pearl caught fire 10 miles off this stretch of coast. The Singapore-flagged container ship was carrying 1,486 containers, including tonnes of hazardous materials such as nitric acid. As the blaze intensified, containers fell overboard and billions of pellets known as nurdles, which are used to make most plastic items, spilled into the sea before the vessel sank.
In the weeks that followed, hundreds of dead marine animals washed ashore, including more than 100 turtles and dozens of dolphins.
“The coconut trees turned black and died. Baby coconuts started falling. We know by experience that this is not normal and was a result of the disaster,” says Roger Peiris, who was working for the YMCA at the time and went on to advocate for fishers and other affected communities to have a greater role in the recovery efforts.
Five years later, nurdles are still washing ashore.
Jude Sulanta, a local fisher, says the problem gets worse during the monsoon season: “The nurdles come to the shore with the strong wind, when the sea is rough. When the sea is calm, they are stuck on the ocean floor.”
Damaged fishing grounds have made livelihoods increasingly difficult to sustain, say many of the fishers. And they are still waiting for compensation.
Those losses sit at the centre of a sprawling legal battle over responsibility. In July 2025, Sri Lanka’s supreme court issued a ruling ordering the companies behind the X-Press Pearl to pay an initial $1bn, with further compensation to be determined. The court also found serious failures by several Sri Lankan state authorities and ordered a fresh investigation into allegations of corruption surrounding efforts to assess and recover compensation.
More than a year later, almost all of the court-ordered sum remains unpaid. The vessel’s owner, X-Press Feeders, and insurer, London P&I, have disputed the ruling and its approach to maritime liability, while talks with the Sri Lankan government continue. A separate compensation case brought by Sri Lanka in Singapore remains active but is on hold pending related proceedings in London.
Although interim compensation was paid for income lost during the post-disaster temporary fishing ban, fishers say the way claimants were classified excluded many of the people affected.
“A lot of genuine fishers missed getting compensation,” says Sulanta.
Several fishers argued that larger operators and well-resourced parts of the industry were better placed to lobby officials, while small-scale fishers lacked the documentation, time or connections to make claims.
“The bigger boats and dry fish industry have better and more influential representation with the authorities,” says Anthony Nishantha, a local fisher who helped lawyers pursuing damages for the disaster. “Us smaller fishers don’t have the same lobbying power.”
An initial assessment by the government-appointed expert panel put the disaster’s environmental damage at $6.4bn (£4.8bn).
“The initial impacts included the direct effects on fishing caused by debris and parts of the damaged ship,” says Prof Prasanthi Gunawardena, an environmental economist and co-chair of the panel. “But based on research from elsewhere, we predicted that there would also be longer-term fishing losses.”
Fishers describe continued damage to fishing nets.
“When the fishing net is cast on the rocks, it pulls something like cotton wool,” Nishantha says. “This started happening with the disaster.”
They suspect contaminants from the spill are responsible, although the cause has not been independently established.
They also describe changes in rocky reefs where fish have traditionally gathered and bred. Knowledge of these grounds has been passed down through generations, allowing fishers to identify fishing areas without GPS technology.
“We are generational fishers,” says Ranga Fernando. “My father showed me where different types of fish gather.”
But, he explains, inherited knowledge has become less reliable since the disaster, as familiar patterns have changed. Nishantha points to Thambugala, a well-known fishing area close to where the vessel went down, where he says fish still gather but no longer appear to breed in the same numbers.
“Even just a few weeks ago, two or three turtles washed up on the shore,” he says. “That is usually very rare, but we are seeing these things more.”
Fishers say the impact on the lagoon in Negombo, which opens into the sea, has received less attention. Jude Anthony, who farms fish there, says nurdles and other pollution inundated his pens after the disaster, killing stock he had spent months raising.
“Everyone is talking about the fish that were destroyed on that day,” he says. “But even now we cannot fish properly.”
The fishers acknowledge that wider pollution from urban development was already affecting the industry. But they believe the X-Press Pearl disaster compounded existing problems. Combined with rising living costs, these pressures have made fishing increasingly difficult to sustain, pushing locals to sell their boats or seek work abroad.
“There are fewer people in the village. They went overseas to support their families,” Sulanta says.
The Centre for Environmental Justice (CEJ), which helped bring the supreme court case, says it is continuing to pursue enforcement of the $1bn ruling. So far, only about $1m has been paid.
“We are in the process of challenging the non-enforcement of the court order, nationally and internationally,” says Hemantha Withanage, co-founder and chair of the CEJ. “This is how corporations discriminate against less powerful developing countries.”
Five years of meetings, claims and uncertainty have left many fishers increasingly disillusioned, while the daily need to earn a living makes the pursuit of justice a luxury they cannot afford.
“No one cares about the little guy,” says Anthony. “We are not educated. We don’t know where to go to speak about these issues, so we are not taken care of. We can’t speak directly with the people at the top, so what more can we do?”
In the end, he says, fishers are left with little choice but to carry on: “We mind our own business, and we work and we live.”
A spokesperson for X-Press Feeders says: “We know and acknowledge that the sinking of the X-Press Pearl had an impact on the environment of Sri Lanka but cannot assume that all nurdles collected today must be originating from the X-Press Pearl incident, not least given there have been other substantial nurdle spills in Sri Lankan waters.”
They add: “We respectfully disagree with the ruling of Sri Lanka’s supreme court and could not make payment because the ruling relied wholly on assessments by Sri Lanka’s Marine Environment Protection Authority that international experts have since discredited. The supreme court also did not consider the ongoing compensation proceedings in Singapore initiated by the Sri Lankan government itself.”
The Sri Lankan government and London P&I did not respond to requests for comment.

title: EU officials reject Cop31 deal as it 'doesn't speak to reality of the climate crisis' – video
article_text:
EU officials reject Cop31 deal as it 'doesn't speak to reality of the climate crisis' – video
The Cop31 climate talks fell into disarray as the EU, UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate. Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, said the EU could not support the proposed deal, in part because it made no mention of fossil fuels. The president of the negotiations, Australia's Chris Bowen, called the failure 'very disappointing', saying that a lot of good work had been done but 'many parties who were people of good faith had very strong red lines on a couple of key issues, and despite many, many attempts … those red lines on behalf of different parties were just not able to be met'.

title: How the war in Iran turned the Gulf into a climate catastrophe – video explainer
article_text:
How the war in Iran turned the Gulf into a climate catastrophe – video explainer
The war between the US, Israel and Iran has turned the strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes, into a battlefield, but also the centre of a deepening environmental disaster. Tankers struck by missiles or sea mines are leaking oil into the Gulf, leaving vast slicks visible from space, staining coastlines and threatening lasting damage to marine ecosystems. Many of these areas remain inaccessible because of the naval blockade, making it virtually impossible to document the devastation on the ground. The Guardian has examined dozens of satellite images and spoken to environmental experts in an effort to assess the scale of the damage

title: IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist
article_text:
Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned.
Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems.
Some countries are holding up work on the three-part report in a row over the body’s role and representation of developing countries. One group has argued that racist assumptions underpin some of the body’s recommendations.
Rockström said the reports were fair. “The IPCC is objective, evidence-based science, and it’s the only thing that we can reliably stand on as a basis for our policymaking,” he said. “The IPCC is the summary of everything done voluntarily by scientists from the entire world, global south and global north, that collectively carries out a synthesis [of established research].”
The IPCC’s work is used to inform the annual climate “conference of the parties” (Cop) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Its next assessment, called AR7, the seventh in a series dating back to 1988, under way, and it is hoped it will be completed in 2028. In the autumn of that year, nations will gather for Cop33, where the second “global stocktake” under the Paris agreement will be thrashed out.
This is the mechanism by which progress towards the core Paris goal, of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, will be judged. The stocktake is almost certain to find that current pledges to cut greenhouse gas emissions are inadequate and must be improved.
The UN has already found the world to be on track for a 2.8C temperature rise, a level previous IPCC reports have found would result in severe and, in some cases, irreversible consequences, such as the melting of ice caps and glaciers, sea level rises, coral bleaching and extreme weather.
But some countries – chiefly Russia, India and the Arab group of countries including Saudi Arabia – want to delay publication of AR7 until 2029, after the global stocktake is completed. They argue, with the backing of some climate campaigners, that developing countries are disadvantaged in trying to submit science to the IPCC. As a result, some claim, the work is permeated by racist assumptions that guarantee the privilege of developed countries.
Lidy Nacpil, the coordinator of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, told the Guardian the IPCC’s scenarios for cutting greenhouse gas emissions – known as “mitigation” in UN jargon – were “biased against the interests of the global south”.
For instance, she said, one assumption was that cutting emissions should be done where it was most cost-efficient. “And where is it cheap to do mitigation? In the global south.” Changing the assumptions would produce different scenarios, Nacpil said.
Nacpil said singling out Saudi Arabia, “whose behaviour we’re not always sympathetic with”, was “also very racist”. She asked: “Who started the fossil fuel industries in this region? Who enjoyed it for now dozens of decades? Whose multinational companies really grew from the extraction of oil and gas in the Middle East? This is not us taking sides. This is us saying: ‘But the pot is calling the kettle black.’ And they’re using their economic, political, and racial power to do this.”
Rockström rejected this. “The pathways to the future represent different socioeconomic realities around the world,” he told the Guardian, in an interview at Cop31. “This is based on the best evidence we have, and this evidence has no north or south bias. It represents the best peer-reviewed science of our understanding of how to close income gaps in poor countries versus rich countries, demographic changes, health projections, and of course also therefore forecasting socioeconomic development. It’s an objective, evidence-based analysis of the reality.”
He added: “We have to defend that objective science. We should not use science as the arena to fight for justice or human rights or even democracy. That’s not the role of science.”
Many other developing countries, including small islands and the least developed countries, have called for the IPCC report to be completed without delay.
Raju Pandit Chhetri, a negotiator from Nepal, said calling the IPCC racist was “a political line”. “What we need to do in this process is really respect the science,” he said. “Coming from Nepal, I can tell you the impacts in just a few hours’ time: losing thousands of lives, let alone billions of pounds worth of property. There are countries who think that making stronger science will put pressure on them to [cut emissions].”
The core committees of the IPCC are run by pairs of scientists, one each from developed and developing countries. China, India and Saudi Arabia all supply leading scientists to the organisation, but insiders acknowledge that parts of the process are dominated by European researchers.
The IPCC said that out of 664 appointed authors working on the drafts of its three working group reports, 51% came from developing countries and economies in transition – an increase of almost half, compared with the last report in 2021. Each chapter across the three reports includes at least one developing-country chapter scientist.
A spokesperson for the IPCC said: “IPCC is absolutely committed to promoting diversity and inclusion and has taken multiple steps to do so during its seventh cycle. As the UN body assessing the science related to climate change, we uphold and stand by the core values of integrity, professionalism and respect for diversity and gender. In the current cycle, the IPCC introduced institutional measures that implement equity and inclusivity.”
Rockström said even if AR7 was delayed, the science in AR6 would be enough to show that current pledges, made last year before Cop30, must be vastly improved. “We have all the evidence we need. Even if you based your updates [on emissions pledges] only on AR6, we would still be making enormous progress,” he said.
Others fear a delay could be used by countries to derail the global stocktake, for instance by arguing it too must be delayed or modified. “It’s throwing more sand in the gears,” one expert involved in the process said.
The row has been going on all year, but is coming to a head because the body meets soon to decide its budget. Although it has reserves of cash to draw on, if a budget cannot be agreed there will be little chance of the IPCC being able to produce its reports before the stocktake.
Technically, the IPCC issues cannot be solved at Cop because they can only be agreed within the body itself, but as governments are meeting in Turkey, some form of compromise may be possible. The chair of the IPCC, the British scientist Jim Skea, extended his attendance at Cop31 for further talks on the issue.
The first draft of the “cover decision” from Cop31, released on Monday, contains references to the need for IPCC science. Though it is likely to be revised several times yet, the draft “recognises the central role of the best available science and of the IPCC” and “recognises the value of a full range of knowledge and participation in the IPCC, including contributions from Indigenous peoples, people of African descent, local communities, non-English speaking regions, and developing countries, and allow sufficient time to prepare comprehensive and credible scientific assessments”.

title: Briton swims length of strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental cost of war
article_text:
A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim in the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.
Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam a 9.3-mile (15km) section of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.
According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, he witnessed several attacks on commercial shipping, explosions in the distance and fighter jets overhead.
An oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 2.5 miles from where he was swimming on the first day. On the second, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from a burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier, Tara Gas, and later he passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.
“My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers onboard,” Pugh said. “The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences, not just for crew members but also on the surrounding marine environment.”
The 56-year-old undertook his first swim in a conflict zone to urge an end to the fighting, the reopening of the strait and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.
Believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the strait since the conflict began in March, Pugh swam a route from Musandam Island, carving through the dramatic mountains and inlets of Oman’s Musandam peninsula to reach the Cape of Hormuz at the peninsula’s northern tip.
He said: “War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes. But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped.”
The small expedition team included a support boat and kayak that remained alongside Pugh during the swim.
Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often received less attention than the human cost. According to the UN, at least 175 vessels have been attacked since fighting began, and about 30 attacks have caused significant pollution.
The strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.
Pugh, who was born in Plymouth, said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

title: Trump defers to appeals court over army plan to detonate bomb-making material in Iowa
article_text:
Donald Trump on Monday halted the planned detonation of several tons of degraded bomb-making material at an Iowa ammunition plant, urging a federal appeals court to first sign off on what he called the safest way to resolve the situation.
“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor-Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump said in a Truth Social post.
The detonation of 68 barrels containing nearly 9,500lb of lead azide held at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant was initially planned for Friday, but the army has since changed the date three times after an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.
They had most recently planned for a detonation this coming Wednesday, saying the weather was most favorable that day.
In a court filing, the US Department of Justice notified the appeals court that the Army would invoke an emergency exception to go ahead with the explosion. But that was challenged in court by the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter, arguing that the EPA had skipped necessary permitting steps.
The court then put an administrative stay on the permit so that it could review the emergency motion. In response, the government said there is “an immediate risk” that the lead will explode as temperatures drop below 30 degrees in the upcoming days.
According to the Des Moines Register, the filing said that the lead azide, an explosive made of lead and nitrogen used primarily in detonators and blasting caps, is more susceptible because the blast doors to bunkers containing the compound had been removed and could not be replaced.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, a small town in southeastern Iowa, where the plant is sited, and thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.
The Army has warned that the blast could release a plume of toxic lead dust extending up to 100 miles northeast, possibly reaching cities such as Wapello and New Boston, Illinois.
Trump said he preferred to take care of the volatile material as soon as possible and that a controlled detonation would be much safer.
Trump said that “experts”, including in the military, “feel that this approach will be a far safer one than allowing the situation to fester, not knowing when they will detonate by themselves. This operation would, in other words, be a controlled one rather than a large, spontaneous explosion.”
The Army has said a controlled detonation “to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion”.
If Sand and the court do not agree, Trump said the administration will have no choice but to not proceed with the planned detonation, adding that he would hold the incoming governor responsible for “any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation”.
